maintopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OF "CANADA" FOR "DOMINION OF CANADA" IN ACTS, ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OF "CANADA" FOR "DOMINION OF CANADA" IN ACTS, ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is that whenever in any act of the parliament of Canada, or in any order of the governor in council, or in any regulation passed pursuant thereto, the expression "Dominion of Canada" is used, there shall be substituted therefor the expression "Canada"; and whenever the expression "dominion" is used there shall be substituted therefor the expression "Canada" or "Canadian" as the case may be.
One of the many reasons for this bill is that since Canada has become a sovereign state the word "dominion" as applied to Canada has entirely lost its original meaning.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Mr.. Speaker, first I should like to express my thanks to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for helping to carry over this debate
Freight Rates

until the provincial premiers had had an opportunity of being heard in Ottawa. I hope that before the debate closes the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) will supplement the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and hold out more hope to the people of Canada than that contained in the Prime Minister's statement.
In this morning's Globe and Mail there is a story from Ottawa, written by Warren Baldwin, to the effect that while in Ottawa the premiers recommended that a royal commission be appointed to investigate the whole question and that pending the royal commission's report the additional rates now in effect be suspended. The royal commission plan involves an investigation of the financial position of both railways, study of the Canadian National capitalization, study of the whole freight rates structure and a reexamination of the evidence and judgment of the board of transport commissioners allowing the present increase.
Also on the front page of the Globe and Mail is a story in connection with the seven cents increase for railroad employees being the board's limit. Some criticism has been made of members of this group for urging that no increase in freight rates be granted while representations are being made for increases in wages. In view of the fact that no increase has been granted to railroad employees for a long time-and the increase in the cost of living has affected these employees as it has all citizens

I do not see that there is any argument about it. The railway employees are entitled to an increase in order to cope with rising costs. In my opinion the Canadian Pacific is in position to pay the increased wages asked for, and the taxpayers of Canada should be prepared if necessary to make it possible for the Canadian National Railways to pay the increased wages.
When I was speaking the other evening I mentioned that again and again throughout the judgment of the board of transport commissioners we read that rates may be increased, may be adjusted, and so on. I expressed the fear that in some parts of Canada where there are already excessively high rates the full 21 per cent increase would be authorized, while in other parts of Canada, where the rates are not so high, no increase would be put into effect. I now have information to support my fears.
For example, the producers at Edenwold have had their rates on eggs increased by 57 per cent whereas the producers in the Ottawa area have no increase in the minimum [Hr. Nicholson.]
rate. I have received a copy of a letter written by the Western Canada Produce Association to the Express Traffic Association in Montreal outlining their position. They point out that for at least fifteen years public and private organizations have encouraged the farmers to improve their breeding stock and to deliver their eggs to market more quickly. The railways have received greatly increased revenues from the shipment of eggs.
It is noted that the producers in the west are being faced with a serious increase. They give a list of seventeen points in Saskatchewan, such as Caron, Mortlach, Chaplin and so on, at varying distances from Moose Jaw, the mileages ranging all the way from 16-2 to 137-1. I find that the freight rate for a thirty dozen crate of eggs is increased 57-1 per cent for the lowest point and 114-2 per cent for the highest, with an average of 85-7 per cent. For the shipment of smaller crates of twelve and fifteen dozen, the lowest increase is 28-6 per cent, the average is 35-7 per cent and the highest 42-8 per cent.
I submit that it is difficult to build a united Canada when there is such discrimination as is shown against these seventeen points in Saskatchewan. They have had these drastic increases while points in the Ottawa valley continue to pay the old rates.
On a number of occasions I have expressed the opinion in this parliament that as Canada has a large investment in the Hudson Bay railroad and the harbour facilities and elevator at Churchill, it is in the interests of Canadians that this line have a fair break. According to my information this particular railroad does not come within the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners and no application was made to have the rates on this line increased. No authorization has actually been given for an increase, but the fact is that freight rates have been increased.
From Regina to Churchill is a distance of 843 miles. The old rate was $2.36 per hundred as compared with the new rate of $2.86. That is broken down as follows: for the 510 miles on the government-owned line south of Churchill the old rate was $1.43, while the rate on the Canadian National line was 96 cents for a distance of 333 miles. On the new basis the rate on the portion on the Hudson Bay railway is being increased from $1.43 to $1.73, and on the Canadian National portion from 93 cents to $1.13. I do not think there is any argument to be advanced with regard to the increase on the portion from Regina to The Pas, but I do not think there is any justification for the increase of rates on the portion from The Pas to Churchill. As I said, this portion of the railway was not covered in the

Freight Rates
application, and no one has any jurisdiction to decide that there should be this increase.
I want to point out that these increases will wipe out any advantage there might have been for Manitoba or Alberta in using the Churchill facilities. It is true that for Saskatchewan it will still be to our advantage to use the Churchill route during the summer months. From Regina to Churchill the first-class rate on the Churchill route will be $2.86 a hundred pounds as compared with $3.93 via Montreal, lake and rail. From Winnipeg to Churchill the rate is $3.60 as compared with $2.83 to Montreal, lake and rail; from Edmonton to Churchill, the rate will be $3.58; whereas from Edmonton to Vancouver the rate will be $3.01. It will still be cheaper to ship from Edmonton to Churchill than from Edmonton to Montreal, but it will be much cheaper to ship from Edmonton to Vancouver.
In view of the special concessions which have been given to Halifax, Montreal and Vancouver, I think it is not unreasonable to ask during this trial period that the government refrain from making it impossible to give this route a fair chance.
In connection with incoming goods, china-ware, for example, the mileage from Regina to Churchill is 845, and the rate is $1.97. From Regina to Montreal the mileage is 1,707, and the rate is only $2.98. From Regina to Halifax the mileage is 2,367, and to Saint John 2,131; the rate is $3.19. If Regina were to enjoy a rail freight rate comparable with the rate to Montreal, Halifax, or Saint John, our importers would be paying the $1.14 rate instead of $1.97. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I want to urge that, before this debate closes the minister assure parliament that he will review this illegal imposition of increased freight rates on the Hudson Bay railway, which is wholly owned by Canada, does not come under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners, and therefore was not up for consideration when the hearings were being held.
As I mentioned before, the Saskatchewan government prepared a great deal of evidence. I think it cannot be disputed that most fair-minded men would agree that no action should have been taken by the government until this case had been studied and the necessary adjustments made. On page 105 of the compilation of the Saskatchewan government's argument before the board is found the following submission:
The province of Saskatchewan submits that, under such circumstances the railway deficit thus hypothetically assumed should, in the national interest and in order that further regional injustices may be avoided, be financed through a national subsidy rather than by an increase in freight rates. It is further submitted that in
the first instance the national subsidy should take the form of a conditional loan. If a railway crisis exists or develops it may be only temporary in nature. A conditional loan, repayable when the situation becomes normal, and with strict supervision during its currency, would seem to meet the circumstances in a reasonable way.
In supporting the Saskatchewan argument, Mr. M. A. MacPherson, the government counsel, made a careful analysis of the financial position of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He argued that the activities of the railway in land, in the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada, in hotels and steamships, should be taken into account in deciding whether the railway was facing bankruptcy or not. Mr. MacPherson asked Mr. Walker, one of the vice-presidents, the following questions regarding Consolidated Mining and Smelting, a subsidiary of the C.P.R., and received the following answers:
Q. I put it to you that the book value of that stock today is $32,000,000? A. You may or may not be right. I would not contradict you.
Q. I put it to you that the market value of that stock today is $148,000,000? A. You may or may not be right again. I would not contradict you, because I do not know.
Q. If I am right, the book value is $32,000, 000 and the market value is $148,000,000, but you are only carrying it in your annual report as an asset of $8,412,000? A. Well, again the accountants will have to justify that.
Q. The return speaks for itself, Mr. Walker?
Then as to the whole financial position, Mr. Walker said, in reply to the following questions:
Q. So we now have you saying that your credit is impaired, yet your funded debt has been cut down from $228,000,000 to $83,000,000 in six years, your reserves have been built up from $91,000,000 to $350,000,000, you are paying less for your money than you have ever paid in the history'of the company, and you are rid of all your high interest-bearing securities; this is right?
A. I will have to answer the questions in pieces. I am afraid, because it is many-barrelled.
Later:	A. That is largely a matter of bookkeeping. the transfer of items from one side of the ledger to the other,-
And so on and so forth. The argument all the way through, I think, convinces most people that the Canadian Pacific even a year ago, when their financial statements were being examined, were in a strong position. But since that time we have had the report of the 1947 operations, and it is clear that there was no justification for the pessimistic view the C.P.R. took. The company were able to pay all the increased costs they have had in connection with their operations. They were able to pay their income taxes to the federal government. They were able to have available for distribution to their shareholders something over
Freight Rates

$16,000,000. Really the company are asking for this increase of 21 per cent so that they will be able to build up a much larger surplus.
In view of the fact that the people in all parts of Canada will be affected by this legislation, I think the representations made by the provincial premiers were not unreasonable. They asked that a royal commission be appointed and that in the meantime we wipe out the 21 per cent increase that has been authorized. If the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific cannot meet their legitimate commitments, I am sure that members in all parts of this house will be prepared to vote necessary subsidies at the proper time.
Before concluding I should like to remind the house that we have had a most unusual procedure in connection with this whole question. Although months were spent in studying the matter, the findings of the board of transport commissioners were not brought down until March 30, 1948. Most hon. members at that time were away from Ottawa visiting their constituencies. I was on my way back when I read of the finding. At the earliest opportunity-on April 5-parliament had this matter brought before it by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Again on April 7, when it was clear that the government was not prepared to delay in one detail, the present amendment was placed before parliament.
I should like to remind the house that section 330 of the Railway Act sets out certain regulations which must be observed when these tariffs are up for revision. Subsection 2 of that section reads:
Upon any such tariff being filed and approved by the board the company shall publish the same, with a notice of such approval in such form as the board directs, in at least two consecutive weekly issues of the Canada Gazette.
I should like the minister to tell the house whether these new tariffs were published for two weeks.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: If I may interrupt the hon. gentleman, I would say the section does not apply to the order issued by the board.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Why not? It is statutory.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Because the order of the board is not only a standard freight rates specification as set out in section 330. If it is, as my hon. friend states, then the order of the board is illegal and the shipper would not have to pay the rates. Let it be tested in the courts; but the counsel of the board of transport commissioners informed me that this section has not been violated.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Again I think I shall have to ask some of my legal friends to come to my assistance, because I do not believe any board has authority to set aside acts of parliament. I shall be surprised if some of the larger shippers do not do as the minister suggests.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: They have not set aside any act of parliament, or any section. The section is there, and it has not been contravened.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
If I understand the English language, this section clearly states what is to be the procedure when new tariffs are introduced. Subsection 4 says:
Until the provisions of this section have been complied with, no toll shall be charged by the company.
Then section 31 deals with special freight tariffs:
Special freight tariffs shall be filed by the company with the board, and every such tariff shall specify the date of the issue thereof and the date on which it is intended to take effect...
3. When any such special freight tariff advances any toll previously authorized to be charged under this act. the company shall in like manner file and publish such tariff thirty days previously to the date on which such tariff is intended to take effect; provided that where objection to any such tariff is filed with the board, the burden of proof justifying the proposed advances shall be upon the company filing said tariff.
I think that type of legislation is reasonable, Mr. Speaker. These companies are public carriers. They not only serve the people in the Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto area; they serve the people of Lintlaw, Hazel Dell and Arran; and the shippers there are entitled to at least thirty days' notice before the rates are changed. They may wish to move their goods by truck, or to make other arrangements; and I do not think the board of transport commissioners or the government should ask parliament to approve changes made so hastily. The decision was reached on March 30. The matter was brought before parliament on April 5, and though representations were made by members of all parties, including their own, particularly by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), two days later the minister rose and said the matter had been considered, that no changes were to be made, but that the new rates were to go into effect immediately. I shall be surprised therefore if the government does not change its mind, if some of the

Freight Rates
firms that are able to engage competent legal advisers do not make a test case of this. The result might be embarrassing to the companies involved, and certainly to the government.
I urge upon the hon. member for Fraser Valley, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) and all the other members from British Columbia and the maritimes on the other side of the house to stand up with us and register this last protest at the failure of the government to meet the requests of seven provinces.

maintopic: SUPPLY' FREIGHT RATES-INCREASES ORDERED BY TRANSPORT BOARD-AMENDMENT, MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there may be discrimina-iton in freight rates. It is possible; but I do not see what a royal commission could do better than the transport board. That board is supposed to do its work properly. The other day the minister spoke plainly about it; he said the transport board would have to consider any discrimination that may exist with respect to freight rates. That is pure horse sense, pure common sense; the transport board is supposed to do some work. If that work is not done properly, or if it is not completed, let them start again; then if they cannot do it, let us fire them. That is an honest view of the whole thing.
The transport board should read the speeches that have been made in this house, especially the one by my good friend who preceded me (Mr. Nicholson). The transport board should read what has been said here with respect to discrimination, and they would do much better than any royal commission. If we have a royal commission it will take a year or so, it will cost a million dollars and will do nothing. How is it my friends of the C.C.F. party are always so ready to defend public servants, yet when there is work to be done by a public servant they say, "Let us have a royal commission"? There should be no royal commission unless it be for the investigation of scandals or something of the kind. The purpose of this board is to inform the government. It is not for us to look into matters of discrimination except when they are mentioned to us by our constituents. I had some discriminations in my constituency, and I complained to the board in due course. I do not pretend that the freight rates are perfect; far from it, but I say the transport commission should have taken the trouble to find out what those discriminations were, without being told each time.
Now, sir, this is the time to vote. We have heard a lot about freight rates from every section of the country, and we cannot learn
any more than we have been told already by
hon. members. We are saturated with this discussion about freight rates. It is not that I do not believe they are important; I think they are important, but the issue is not freight rates. The issue is a vote of confidence in the government. If this house has confidence in the government we will have the support of the majority of the house. speechtext:
Before Your Honour leaves the chair there is another matter about which I should like to speak at this time, exercising the ancient right of a private member to air grievances before the house goes into committee of supply. This is indeed the first opportunity that I have had to discuss this matter since it was precipitated by the action of the government in the tabling of certain orders in council by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) on April 19. The matter referred to in these orders in council, and about which I wish to speak, is the action of the government in making certain changes by order in council with reference to government annuities.
As everyone knows, the action taken by the government was, in the main, to change the rate of interest on the basis of which the annuity tables are calculated. The rate was changed from four per cent to three per cent. The result of that change, along with other changes made at the same time, is that Canadian government annuities as from April 19, 1948, cost more to Canadians who wish to purchase them. In my view, Mr. Speaker, this action of the government is a blow at social security which is hard to understand at this stage of our national development.

Government Annuities
Despite the differences that might obtain amongst the various parties in this house as to ways and .means of achieving social security, there is general agreement that we should move in that direction. There is also general agreement that a plan of old age security involving contributions by citizens themselves, by employers in certain cases, and by the government is all to the good. Therefore I say it is hard to understand the government, at this stage of our national development, when the people of Canada are calling for better old age security, taking this action which has the effect of striking a blow at one very good plan that has been on our statute book since 1908.
The effect of this decision by the government is best seen when one considers the group plans that are taken out, by arrangement with Canadian government annuities, bj' employers on behalf of their employees. Most people imagine that government annuities are mainly taken by individuals. The fact is that there are more individual contracts than there are group certificates thus far, but the number of individuals included in group contracts has been increasing very rapidly during recent years. As at March 31, 1947, there were in existence 194,623 contracts. Of these, 108,625 were held by individuals by direct arrangement with the annuities branch; S5,99S were held by individuals through the medium of group plans taken out by employers on behalf of their employees.
With reference to the number of individuals in group plans, may I point out that in 1945, 9,313 individuals were enrolled in group plans. In 1946 the number enrolled in group plans was 17,355; in 1947 it was 30,411. In other words, despite the fact that very little publicity was given to .this excellent plan, its use has been greatly increased in recent years, and all the evidence seems to suggest that still greater use was being made of it in recent months, and still greater use was in store as time went on. But the action of the government in reducing the interest rate, or increasing the cost of these annuities, will have not only the effect of discouraging individuals from taking out government annuities but will definitely discourage	employers-companies
and corporations, large or small-from interesting themselves in what is no longer an attractive plan.
When you look at the group arrangement to which I am referring at the moment you realize immediately that it is a three-way contribution plan. The employee makes a contribution; his employer makes a contribution, and thus far the government has been making a contribution. That contribution has been in two parts. On the one hand, the government has paid the administrative cost of the plan, and on the other hand, by computing the value of annuities on a four per cent interest basis, which is a little higher than the normal interest rate on government bonds, the government has in fact been making a cash contribution to the fund itself.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if any member went out on the street and asked any ordinary citizen of Canada what would be the best kind of old age security plan, in most cases the answer would be: Let us have a three-way contribution-contributions from employee, employer and the government. That is what we have had in this very plan. But the effect of the government's action is to take away the contribution that was being made to the scheme by the government. It is true that the government will still pay the cost of administering the plan, and it is also true that it will still pay what is involved in computing the value of the annuity at three per cent; but, after all, that is not paying anything to the annuitants. That is simply paying the going rate of interest on borrowed money.
Not only does it have the effect to which I have just referred of striking a blow at the one kind of plan which everybody supports, but it also sets up discrimination between different employees working for the same firm. I will not mention the name of the company, but the bread man who calls at our home in Winnipeg has told me about his company being in this plan. He has an individual contract within a group plan. His contract, of course, was issued prior to April 19, and therefore he gets the advantages of the old rate; but a new employee of the same bread company who may be delivering bread over on the next street next week will have to have his pension with that company computed on the basis of a new rate; he will have to pay more for the same rate of pension. It is perfectly true that contracts that were in effect prior to April 19 suffer no change, but individual contracts that are written after April 19, or the contracts of employees in groups, where the individual enters even an established plan after April 19, must come under the new rate; and so I point out that discrimination between employees working for the same firm will result from this decision.
There has been considerable reference to this in the newspapers, both before and after the event. Papers like the Toronto Star, for example-I will not take time to read the quotation-have pointed out that by this
3360
Government Annuities

action companies are already being discouraged from going ahead with plans they had in view. I would point out that what this means is not that annuities of this description will be written by the insurance companies; it means that they will not be written at all. What I have said about group plans points up the issue in terms of the over-all picture, because, as I say, the whole country is looking toward a threeway contributory scheme.
It is also true with respect to individuals who have suffered a sad blow in their aim of achieving social security. I think of the large number of self-employed persons, of professional men-even members of parliament- who have no pension scheme which can be carried on on a three-way basis. Prior to April 19 they at least had a chance of entering into a two-way plan that was really worthwhile.
I hold in my hand just about the only piece of advertising that was circulated by the annuities branch prior to April 19. It is an attractive booklet headed, "Canadian government annuities," and below that appears a picture of the parliament building. Then underneath is the caption, "Backed by the whole resources of the dominion." On page 3 there are the following two paragraphs:
If you are a young man or woman this little booklet carries to you a wonderful opportunity to secure comfort and independence in your old age. Read every word of it. Bear in mind that, if you would have an old age free from want or dependence, you must save and invest wisely in your youth.
If you are an older man or woman with limited capital, and your earning days are over, this booklet carries a message of comfort and cheer. It tells how you can invest your capital in a way which will give you a safe, steady and dependable income for the rest of your life-an income guaranteed by the entire Dominion of Canada.
If this was not the last copy of the book that I possess I would tear it up right here, because that is what the government has done with this most attractive plan.
The argument is sometimes advanoed that the change to which I refer had to be made to put the annuities fund in a proper actuarial position. It was said that it was not proper for the government to pay what amounted to four per cent on the money paid in by annuitants when it could borrow money in the open market or on government bonds at three per cent.
I submit that that argument misses the whole point and purpose of Canadian government annuities. This was not something actuarially unsound; it was-and deliberately so-a straight government contribution in the interests of old age security. Everyone knows the way it worked. The payments that were made went

into the consolidated revenue fund, and when an annuity was paid it was paid out of the consolidated' revenue fund. At the present time the amounts being paid in are greatly in excess of the amounts being drawn out; the only separateness about this is in terms of bookkeeping.
Let me remind the house and the government that the purpose of government annuities was set out in the preamble to the original bill, which was passed in 1908-for back in those days bills had preambles to indicate their purpose. This is chapter 5 of the statutes of Canada for 1908, being 7-8 Edward VII. The preamble reads:
Whereas it is in the public interest that habits of thrift be promoted and that the people of Canada be encouraged and aided thereto so that provision may be made for old age; and whereas it is expedient that further facilities be afforded for the attainment of the said objects:	Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows-
Then follows the act itself.
The purpose was to encourage thrift and the making of provision for old age. Part of the purpose was to provide facilities to make that possible. The providing of facilities did not mean just the employment of a bookkeeper; it meant the providing of the necessary contributions to set up an attractive plan. I hope hon. members will pardon my making a somewhat personal reference, but in studying the origins of this act I confess that I ran across something that interested me in a personal way. I found that the second reading of the bill was moved, the debate thereon took place, the bill was considered in committee and reported all on June 18, 1908. That was the very day on which I was born. Little did I realize when I was howling in my crib that forty years later I would be howling in defence of an act passed in this house that very day.
The bill was piloted through the house by Mr. Fielding, minister of finance in the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. This was just a few months before the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was first elected to the house. Mr. Fielding pointed out at that time that in the bill presented to parliament there was a small element of government subsidy or government assistance. Even in those days there were a few members who hoped that the bill was not going to provide competition for the insurance companies. Mr. Fielding answered that while they were not paying very much by way of subsidy, to the extent that they were paying four per cent on the money invested rather than three per cent, there would be that

Government Annuities
element of government assistance toward achieving the objectives set out in the preamble which I have just read.

When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) defended this action the other day he referred to the rate that the government paid on Dominion of Canada bonds, namely, three per cent, and said that the effect of this order in council was to put government annuities on a parallel basis with Dominion of Canada bonds. I submit that that argument does not hold at all, that you are dealing with two different things. If this government were selling bonds which could not be redeemed except in small amounts in later years or at death they would not be able to sell them at a three per cent interest rate. That is what you have with an annuity. An annuity is not something with an immediate cash surrender value; it is to make provision for old age and is on an entirely different 5849-214J
basis. As I say, if bonds were on that basis you would not be able to sell them at three per cent.
One other argument which is frequently made is that the rate that was paid involved a subsidy. It is strange how many there are in the house who, whenever a subsidy is offered with which they do not agree, get up and argue against the general principle of paying subsidies at all, and yet in some cases readily agree to a subsidy payment. In this connection may I read a paragraph, commenting on the action of the government-not on the action of the house, Mr. Speaker-from the Toronto Daily Star of April 20? This, I may say, was on the financial page and was written by the financial editor:
Business is very apt today at criticizing government subsidies to the people. The fact remains, however, that business itself is not adverse to soliciting government help in reaching an objective it considers desirable. The subsidy to gold mines is but one of many instances where this principle applies.
Another is the government guarantee of loans made by insurance companies under the National Housing Act. To encourage home construction, a desirable social objective, the government assumes the risk for the entire loan although the insurance companies nevertheless receive a five per cent return on the money they advance.
I contend that those who argue against government annuities on the old basis by saying that they involved a subsidy, are not putting up an effective argument at all. Our economy is full of the paying of subsidies of all kinds, and I suggest there is no worthier objective for the paying of subsidies than that of providing old age security.
It strikes me as strange that this action of the government in reducing the value of government annuities, thus striking a blow at this form of security, should come at a time when so much use was being made of this plan. I have already given some figures with respect to individuals in group plans. May I give a few more figures and show that in recent years this was becoming a very popular arrangement. First of all, may I say that back in 1925 the total number of contracts taken out-now I am giving total figures, both individual and group-was only 486; in 1930 it was 1,257; in 1935, 3,930; in 1940, 9,014; in 1945, 15,796; in 1946, 25,538, and in 1947, 43,585. Those figures, I may say, are in each case for the year ended March 31 of the year indicated. The last figure I was able to get was for the year ended March 31, 1947. I do not know how many were taken out in the year ended March 31, 1948. But it seems strange that just when it is getting popular, just when the people of Canada are realizing
Government Annuities

what a good thing this is, the government strikes the blow it has struck.
May I read a word or two from Mr. Fielding back on the day to which I referred, June 18. 1908, when he said this, as reported at column 10851 of Hansard for that year:
The mere fact that a thing is good in itself does not mean that it will be taken up by the public. Even the best things of life have to be recommended. Although I believe this to be an excellent scheme, founded on sound principles and calculated to do much good. I do not anticipate that the public will rush after it unless somebody takes pains to explain its merits and advantages.

They indicated it was a change which wras coming soon. I saw one report somewhere which suggested that the matter of annuities was to be transferred from the Minister of Labour to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Now let me turn to deferred life annuities. First I will take the instance of a male aged thirty purchasing an annuity of $100 to commence at sixty-five guaranteed for ten years. It used to cost $15.06 a year; it now costs $20.50 a year, an increase of 36 per cent. A female aged twenty buying a $100 annuity to commence at age sixty, guaranteed for ten years, used to have to pay $14.37 a year. Now it is $20.64, an increase of 43 per cent. I might go on and give other figures, but they run in these general brackets. In the immediate annuities there is an increase of 15 or 16 per cent, while in the deferred annuities the increase runs from 36 to about 44 per cent.
These rate changes are due in part, as I have said already, to the withdrawal of the contribution by the government to this two or three way scheme, which is what results from the reduction of the rate from four per cent to three per cent. The rate changes result as well from a change in mortality tables, this also being done by order in council. These tables are worked out by actuaries, and the government decided to use a certain table, namely the mortality of annuitants, 1900 to 1920, published by the institute of actuaries in Scotland, known as-well, there is a long list of letters here-with an arbitrary reduction of three years in the age. In other words the government has conformed to the general pattern of the insurance companies, and the fact of the matter is that insurance companies have to set their actuarial rates to include their extra costs and profits, which are not necessary in the case of the government scheme. Therefore the point the minister interjected a moment
ago is also one about which I complain. I do not complain about people living longer, as he says, but I do complain as to the basis upon which the actuarial change has been made.
Not only have there been these changes in rates and tables; there have also been changes in the regulations. For example, one of the outstanding features about government annuities thus far has been the right of purchasers to pay odd amounts and at odd times. I have in my hand my own little pass book-having started to purchase an annuity some time ago so that this contract is not affected by the change-and in it I note that payments of twenty-five cents and upwards will be received from any annuitant. It is well known that under the old plan you could make such payments of odd amounts at any time and at any post office in Canada. Now a change has been made, which is set out in this document; which reads as follows:
New contracts will not permit deposits of odd amounts at odd times. Purchasers will be expected to follow the prescribed schedule of premium payments. Provision will be made for the payment of arrears within reasonable limits, and the prepayment of premiums will be allowed by special arrangement.
I have no doubt there have been abuses of that generous privilege under the old contracts, but it seems to me the attempt to correct abuses has led the government too far the other way, and has turned what was a simple, attractive plan into something that will require the purchaser to meet his payments regularly and will frighten many people away from taking it on lest it become a commitment they might not be able to keep up. The regulation to which I have just referred suggests that the government annuities branch may accept payments in arrears, but under conditions we do not yet know. In other words the whole thing is being hamstrung and changed from an attractive, simple, popular plan into something that just will not appeal to people at all.
Here is where I think my private enterprise friends should listen. This does not mean that annuities of this kind will now be sold by the insurance companies. Everyone knows the insurance companies could not possibly meet these terms. What it means, however, is that this sort of thing will not be done at all, and that we shall have had a set-back in our hopes of developing a reasonable plan for social security.
I am afraid my time is just about up, and I had better come to a conclusion. I have had a great many representations about this matter since the tabling of the order in council on April 19. I have had resolutions
Government Annuities

had earlier. Again, under the present proposal it would appear that anyone who buys will not receive as much for his investment as would have been obtained earlier. That does not seem fair; we all try to get a fair deal.
Suppose one of these gentlemen I refer to is drawing an annuity of $100 a month, or $1,200 a year, which is the maximum; then, if a month or two hence someone else wants to buy an annuity under the amended scheme, he would not be able to get the same return as the person who bought an annuity a short time ago. That does not seem to me to be fair on the part of the government, because everybody should be treated the same way. I have only praise for Canada's government annuity program which has been in operation for quite a long time. It has promoted thrift in Canada and given a feeling of security and safety to those who have invested in it.
I am not conversant with the whole program, but having listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who apparently is conversant with it, I would urge the government to reconsider any proposal which would retard or slow up the purchase of annuities by the average citizen. A government annuity is one thing in which the average humble citizen can invest with a feeling of safety and security. I am not suggesting, of course, that annuities sold by large insurance companies are not safe or secure; I will go so far as to say that they are. But, after all, there is nothing better than an annuity contract with the government, because the whole country stands back of it.

Many people today will tell you that what is growing up in Canada is a managerial form of society in which the government are managed from the outside to the detriment of the people.
When the government annuity scheme was started away back in 1908 a definite rate of interest was fixed. That is now being changed by making the rate one per cent lower, which is equivalent to stepping up the premium by 25 per cent. Surely if the government was liberal enough in 1908 to lay the basis for an annuity scheme which would be available to the people of this country, it must recognize that the step it is now taking is retrogressive and might well have been initiated by the Conservative party. That just bears out my contention that what has happened in, this country is that the Conservative party has disappeared, and the Liberals have gone Conservative.

Their actions in the house and in the country demonstrate that. I say the timing of this measure is bad and, along with other steps which the government has taken, it indicates that the government is being pushed from outside. My guess is as good as anyone else's and it is that the old line insurance companies fear the development of government insurance because they cannot compete with it. Saskatchewan in the field of automobile insurance and fire insurance has demonstrated that the government can give better service and better protection at cheaper rates than the old line insurance companies, and the insurance companies want to offset that development.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has pointed out, the

Government Annuities
fear of insecurity is what everyone in this world has been struggling against and suffering from., not just for generations but for centuries. We have now entered a period in the history of this country where provincial governments and industries are trying to evolve some scheme of protection for the average worker. Let me give the minister an illustration that the change he is making shows bad timing so far as the industry I am going to mention is concerned.
The minister knows that the mining industry in this country never had a pension plan, despite the fact that, as far back as 1920, I know of my personal knowledge that we approached the provincial government time after time for a three-way pension echeme, but we did not succeed in selling it to the government. But away back in 1923 and 1924 the company instituted an anaemic scheme of their own. Nevertheless, though it was anaemic, t'he company did something, and they bore the whole load. Only a year ago some 1,500 employees of that mining industry in Nova Scotia who had reached the age of sixty-five were laid off, and because there was no three-way contributory retirement scheme, the company made these employees a grant, which they call a pension, and which ranges all the way from $16 to $70 a month, based on length of service and a percentage of the average earnings for the last ten years. But a miner's last ten years' earnings would be largely from piecework; it would be the lowest period of his earnings. So the pensions are very small.

Not being actively engaged in that occupation, I let those who are make the decision. Why I hate to see this change made in the government annuity scheme at this time is, among other reasons, the fact that the miners' union and the provincial government have for the last six months been engaged in negotiations to evolve a threeway scheme which will not only protect the miner in the future but also do something for that large group of miners who have been retired' with no adequate pension. Many of these men still have families on their hands and homes to maintain with the income I
have just indicated. This kind of thing, which is a trend away from the three-way pension scheme that protects the average person in the country and gives him an opportunity to participate, is being discouraged. With this measure we are farther back in this field than we were in 1908.
To establish in the industry that I arr talking about the kind of scheme which will protect those who are now out, and those who may come in in the future, will require a contribution from some source of about $12,000,000 to lay a base for a three-way contributory plan. If that is done, if the fear of insecurity, when a person is no longer productive, is removed you remove a lot of the fear of these changes that are talked about which we do not like to see, because insecurity is what drives people toward any kind of solution of the problem where they see themselves on the scrap heap, and are no longer able to produce themselves.
Instead of starting on the road to abandon a very good scheme which covered only a small percentage of the people of this country-it is a very small percentage of the people of the country who can come under the government annuity scheme-we should be trying to improve it.
Let me say this with regard to most industrial workers and, I think, farmers in the country. They are not in a position to carry any kind of insurance with the old line companies. The best they can do is to take a $1,000 policy payable to the beneficiary when they die, and pay on it monthly. When they pass away there is enough left to pay the funeral expenses. They live day by day and pay that kind of insurance, which is the most expensive kind of insurance, against the time when they pass away, so that their families may not go into debt for funeral expenses. That is the only kind of insurance that the average low income person in this country is able to get and pay for with the old line companies.
Rather than do what we are doing now, in effect, stepping up the premium on government annuities by 25 per cent, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) should be bringing in a bill making this plan of government annuities still more available to the people of the country, by reducing the premium and by advertising it widely and incorporating in the national government annuity scheme the industrial workers across the country who are trying to get into some kind of three-way contribution scheme with the companies across the country. I am sure you would get co-operation from the industrialists, and I am absolutely certain that you would get it from the industrial workers.
Government Annuities

When you have 100 or 200 schemes operated separately by each industry in the country the administrative costs are terrific. But if it were centralized with the central government with the staff that is now available, with the scheme brought up to date and the administration done from here and the people of the country covered under this scheme, it would cheapen the administration and it would- guarantee the solvency of the fund because the government would be behind it. Proper audits would be made from time to .time and, regardless of whether the old line companies like it or not, it would not be competing with them, because they certainly cannot give this kind of insurance.
I see in this scheme the basis for the expansion of a well developed three-way contributory scheme which would take care of both farmers and industrial workers either individually or co-operatively. I seriously suggest to the minister that he not go ahead with this thing at this time. This is thought about a lot in the country. Over the week end I had a meeting in Hamilton, praising the government, of course.

When it comes to the matter of annuities, that is the only type of investment in which the small income earner has a chance to invest. Where else can a man with a salary of $35 a week invest his meagre savings and get four per cent interest? There is not another place unless he wants to invest in government bonds, and those are not now for sale. More than that, he would have received only three per cent on them.
I have discussed this question on other occasions with insurance companies, and one of the things they have always beefed about was the fact that the government was selling annuities which would give a return of four per cent. They said frankly that they did not intend to go out and sell annuities against the government, because they could not get a sufficient return or the return to which they thought they were entitled.
When it comes to the general field of life insurance, the government is not in competition with the life insurance companies, and of course they can go ahead in that field.

Saskatchewan Federated Co-operatives
In fact I think it is a healthy thing to have the government selling annuities paying four per cent in competition with insurance companies. It is not like taking over a monopoly. I do not think it is comparable with out and out socialism. It is a form of competition. In that way I think there is a good control of private insurance companies, so that they will endeavour to keep their rates down as low as possible.
We hear a great deal about people being encouraged to invest their savings in order to protect them in their old age. I think that is a good thing. The minister himself spoke about contributory old age pensions. How are people to contribute if they have not sufficient income on which to live? Last year when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) brought his budget down, he told us that over fifty per cent of the people in Canada were living on less than $1,500 a year, if married, and on $750 a year, if single. When you find a condition like that in the country, how do you expect for one moment that these people will be able to get the money to invest in contributory old age pensions or any other compulsory contributory scheme the government may have in mind?
I would not say that the government has had pressure brought to bear on it, or that the minister particularly has had pressure brought to bear upon him from the insurance companies, but I will say this definitely; the insurance companies have been complaining strongly against the government's selling these annuities, thereby allowing room for the small investor to get a four per cent return on his money. I think the minister himself is aware of that fact. That does not necessarily mean to say that they came to him with a written complaint; but I am sure the minister is too smart a man not to know that the insurance companies have been bitterly opposed to the government's selling annuities bearing four per cent interest.
So far as the matter of taking money out of the general revenue is concerned, I think the minister said that on March 31, 1943, approximately half a million dollars was taken out-$497,000, to be exact-and that in March, 1947, $997,000 was taken out. What do we pay each year for family allowances? That money comes out of the general revenue. It comes out of taxation. Will the minister stand up here and say that we should not have family allowances? If he made such a statement as that, I am afraid the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) might ask him to take a vacation. If the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) can logically say he thinks the annuities branch should be put on such a sound financial basis that it should be run with no contribution from the general treasury, then all these other things which I have mentioned-and which the government has sponsored-should be put on exactly the same basis.
I think the time was certainly not opportune for the government to lower this interest rate from four per cent to three per cent. We expect the people of this country to look after themselves in their old age. Almost everyone who has spoken for years past in this house has advocated that procedure. Yet we take away one of the opportunities for people to do that. I want to protest against the government's taking this action at this time. It is most inopportune and it will not work in the best interests of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Yes, it pays all taxes except municipal taxes; that is a matter which is one of controversy at the present time, and I understand that payments will be made in lieu of them, in agreement with the municipalities.
The matter I wish to introduce this afternoon is opportune now after I have spent these few minutes in the way I have. I am glad to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his place before I bring it up. It has to do with the matter of the supply of hardware, particularly nails, to one of our big Saskatchewan co-operative associations, namely, the Saskatchewan Federated Co-operatives Limited. This is an institution which has been built up over the years by the same process that governments here and in other places have advised the people to undertake. They have said the same as the Minister of Labour said a while ago, that people should help themselves when they are in extremities. The people of Saskatchewan have in a variety of ways set up organizations by which they hope to help themselves. They do not consider it fair when obstacles are placed in their way that prevent them from helping themselves as they should be permitted to do.
The file of correspondence I have here is between the president of the Saskatchewan Federated Co-operatives Limited, Mr. George Urwin, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and it also contains letters between the steel controller of Canada, Mr. Fred Ashbaugh, and Mr. C. H. Millard of the united steelworkers of America. The reason that correspondence enters the picture will become apparent as I go along. This co-operative has a membership of around 75,000 people, of whom about 96 per cent are farmers. It is not a corporation in the sense that people have invested money in it for the purpose of making money out of their investment. It is a co-operative in which people have invested money for the purpose of building certain things to serve themselves.
They have done that in this way. They have built 540 retail outlets which service every

populated area in Saskatchewan. Through the affiliation of those 540 retail outlets they have ownership in the central organization, the federated co-operatives limited, through which they operate two coal mines at Drum-heller, a lumber mill at Canoe, British Columbia, an oil refinery at Regina, a flour mill at Outlook and two feed plants, one at Saskatoon and the other at Regina.
As I say, they have done these things to service themselves. They are asking no favours from anybody. They simply want to be able to use their purchasing power in that way, to go into the market and purchase their supplies from manufacturers, or to purchase the raw materials from the suppliers and make them available in consumable form through these outlets. Last year they did a business which would not be considered much in big business circles but which was very satisfactory to them, a business of around $11,500,000; but they are unable to get some supplies, one of the most important of which is nails.
The subject matter of the correspondence I have here is a request to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (a) to make it possible for this organization to buy its portion of the available supply of nails from the present distributors, or (b) to make available 300 tons of steel wire to a firm in Galt which is willing to make these nails for them, provided that it can get the steel wire with which to do so. These are their two requests. The replies are, of course, the same kind the minister has given the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) when he has asked about nails. The minister has given a short, rather abrupt answer, which in most instances could be described as a brush-off. That is about the tone he takes in his replies to the president of this co-operative institution.
Then the Canadian director of the united steelworkers of America, Mr. C. H. Millard, took up the matter on behalf of the cooperative, with which he had some correspondence. Mr. Millard got in touch with the steel controller in an endeavour to have these necessary supplies made available to the firm which is willing to manufacture the nails, but Mr. Ashbaugh has been no more considerate than the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for the obvious reason that he is under the direction of the minister and therefore, I suppose, can do nothing the minister will not permit him to do. Mr. Millard pointed out that a great deal of our iron ore goes to the United States, and for that reason we should be able to get larger supplies of the finished steel. The minister and the controller replied that the shortage of steel would make it impossible

Saskatchewan Federated Co-operatives
to provide the 300 tons required for the manufacture of these nails.
Just on that point, I remember that back in 1942 a request was made by some people in British Columbia who believed there were deposits of iron ore and coal sufficiently close together to make it possible to put up smelters and manufacture steel products there. At that time they were told that there has always been a surplus of steel in Canada, and as a result they were not given permission to do as they wished. If that permission had been given at that time, perhaps the condition of which I speak today would not have arisen. That permission not having been given, however, we now face this shortage; and I claim it is the responsibility of the government either to make this quantity of raw material available for the manufacture of the nails required by this co-operative institution, or to see that the distributors make available to the cooperative enough nails out of the total going into the retail trade to supply their members.
Of course the minister and others will take the position that this would be interfering with private business; but I claim that when seventy-five thousand people have clearly stated by their membership in this organization that they want to do their retail trading in their own stores, they should not be compelled by some business circumstance to go to another person, who certainly would be a competitor of the co-operative institution, in order to buy their nails. If we believe in free enterprise in this country we should certainly make an effort to see that those who engage in it are able to practise that principle through whatever channels they consider are proper and lawful.
I had hoped that the Minister of Agriculture would give some attention to this matter. As everyone knows, he has risen in this chamber on more than one occasion and said that he and his Liberal party in Saskatchewan and here fathered the co-operatives. As a matter of fact, on one occasion he made the statement, "We built the co-operatives". I take issue with that statement, because it is not correct; but if he believes it to be correct-and he would not have said so if he did not believe it-certainly he should do his utmost to let his brainchild grow. Those of us who come from Saskatchewan find it difficult to realize that the government can be so inconsiderate as to permit a lusty baby in the co-operative family to be denied the food necessary to continue its growth in this country of free enterprise. Someone says the child is now bigger than its father. That is so in Saskatchewan;
whether it is true here remains to be seen. I do not want to make an unpleasant political issue of this, but the government say they believe in free enterprise, that they believe in people helping themselves.

The minister repeats that he believes in co-operatives. That is splendid. If the government believe in these three things; if they believe in free enterprise, if they believe people should help themselves by their own free enterprise, and if they believe in co-operatives-which I think the minister will agree are a democratic and sound type of free enterprise-then I say this government should not permit either their own policies or the policies of private business to prevent this enterprise of which I speak from obtaining its share of the available supplies of the goods it requires to satisfy the needs of its membership. The minister could, I think, do a lot to convince the government that that situation could and should be taken care of by his administration.
I do not know that I can give any more convincing arguments than I have given. I have just one further quotation which I think might be brought to the attention of the house. This is from a letter addressed to Mr. Charles Millard from Mr. F. K. Ashbaugh, the steel controller, wherein he says:
In view of the fact that we are not giving assistance in procurement to more than an infinitely small percentage of Canadian industry.. .
This indicates that they are giving some assistance in the matter of procurement. And the very fact that they are doing that indicates to me that it is their duty to make supplies available to this organization about which 1 have spoken today. They have not asked much. They need a great deal more in the hardware line, such things as wire and other metal retail objects. However, they have stated clearly that rather than press the point, to the embarrassment of the country, they will be happy for this year at least to have these 300 tons of steel wire made available to this firm in Galt so that they can manufacture nails. I say the government should proceed immediately to see that this firm gets what it asks, or to see that private industry makes available to the Saskatchewan Federated Co-operatives Limited its share of nails, which will come through the retail trade and which the farmers will buy anyway, because they must have nails to carry out their operations.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) has put the case so well that I wish only to add my voice to what he has said. It is true that the Saskatchewan Federated Co-operatives Limited has its headquarters in my city and that I have been interested in its growth over a number of years.
This is not the first time that this firm, if I may so describe it, has had its troubles in matters of supply. In 1946 I tried to obtain from the wartime prices and trade board a proper quota on canned milk for this co-operative. I have here a letter which advanced the argument against the distribution of canned milk to this organization. This letter, signed by the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew), parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, states:
I have taken the matter up with the wartime prices and trade board, and am advised that under their policy of equitable distribution, evaporated milk is one of the items which continues to be classified as in such serious short supply that it may only be distributed to basic period customers in quantities related to their basic period purchases.
The situation in regard to nails is much the same today, and it is with that argument of the ' government, as set forth in the letter I have just read, and which refers to basic period customers, that I find fault.
Let me put to the house a ridiculous case. We will consider two rival business institutions on two corners of a street. One of these loses all its customers to the other, but the government persists in supplying with the goods the one losing its customers, while the other firm which now has the customers can obtain no goods with which to supply them. Perhaps that is going far afield, and may be considered a ridiculous case. But it will at least point up the fact I wish to make clear. Here is an institution which has been growing in membership but which cannot get supplies. The hon. member for Swift Current put the number of shareholders in the organization at 75,000. I have a statement here from the Cooperative Union of Saskatchewan which states:
Allowing for duplication of membership, it is safe to say that some 300,000 Saskatchewan people are members of one or more co-operatives.
This may be considered a startling statement, particularly to some of my hon. friends to my right. However, that is the way in which we are now doing business in Saskatchewan, on a co-operative basis. There are, of course, reasons why we are operating in that way.

But to get back to my argument, I think the basis of distribution should be one of population or customers who buy goods from a firm. If this particular firm can show a membership of 75,000, and potential purchasers numbering 300,000, I say that firm should receive a great deal of consideration when it comes to a matter of supply.
As my hon. friend pointed out, people started these institutions to help themselves. Here is an organization which says, "We have no nails; nails cannot be obtained." The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) would support me in this. They say, "All right; we have no nails; we will make them." Then they proceed to negotiate to buy unused machinery which will be shipped out to them so that they can make their own nails, if the government will only guarantee a supply of steel from which the nails can be made.
Then the government comes along and says, "No; already all the nails which can be made are being produced. Why should you make nails out there?" I have tried to explode that argument, and I believe I have done so successfully. If the customers are there, then those customers are entitled to their proportion of nails, on any basis of need or equitable distribution.
In connection with canned milk, about which there was discussion a couple of years ago, I have reason to believe that the distribution was not equitable. Is it not ridiculous that a man who buys his groceries at a co-operative store should be permitted to fill his basket or the back of his car-we used to do that, but now a brown parcel will hold the lot of it-and then if he wishes to buy canned milk find that he has to go to some other store to make the purchase? Is that not ridiculous? I believe I have said sufficient, and practically all I had intended to say. I would ask that it be called six o'clock.
