He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house is exactly the same as Bill No. 154 of the last session of parliament. I moved the second reading of that bill on May 9, 1947, but unfortunately it never came up for disoussion again. In support of last year's bill I asked the house to give it favourable consideration as I believed that the vast majority of the Canadian people are in favour of abolishing appeals to the privy council and setting up our own final and ultimate court of appeal for Canada, because it is the next important and logical step toward Canadian sovereignty. I still believe this to be the case, and I am convinced that the vast majority of the Canadian people are today of the same frame of mind.
I have had an opportunity during the recess, since last July, of discussing this question with many people in all walks of life and of different shades of political affiliation, not only in wrestern Canada but in other parts of Canada, and I feel safe in saying that in presenting the bill for the second time to this house for its favourable consideration and support I have most Canadians with me.
Even among the members of my own profession, particularly in the west, I find a preponderance of opinion that we ought to be sufficiently grown up and emancipated to administer and interpret our own laws, and that our supreme court should be the final court of appeal in our own country.
At the last session I based my argument for support almost entirely on the fact that Canada is now a sovereign nation, and this alone should be sufficient for this house to pass this bill. I again make this plea with all sincerity.
Supreme Court Act Amendment

and at this time I shall go farther and argue that our present position in this matter is incompatible with our status as a member of the British commonwealth of nations and as a member of that larger body, the united nations.
Someone said, improperly I believe, that the privy council, in deciding that Canada possessed the power to abolish appeals to that body, signed its own death warrant as a Canadian court. I cannot look at the matter in that way. The spirit in which this famous judgment was rendered is something entirely different from the spirit of a death warrant. It was rather the spirit of a new life; it was an enthusiastic invitation to Canada to assert its sovereignty and to pass this very bill which is now before us. It was an invitation to enjoy that new sovereign life, which in reality we were capable of possessing since the Statute of Westminster was passed in 1931.
To make my point clear, namely that I can read an invitation into the language of the judgment, listen to some of the passages of the judgment as delivered by Lord Jowitt, the Lord Chancellor:
No other solution is consonant with the status of a self-governing dominion . . .
Later on:
It is not consistent with the political conception -which is embodied in the British commonwealth of nations that one member of that commonwealth should be precluded from setting up, if it so desires, a supreme court of appeal having jurisdiction both ultimate and exclusive of any other member.
Later again:
That natural attribute of a sovereign power (namely the establishment of a general court of appeal) stands unqualified and absolute.
While it would have been improper for that body to suggest action, it seemed to me that the general tenor of the language used implies an invitation to apply immediately the law upon which they had adjudicated, because our present position in still maintaining the right of appeal to the privy council is, in the language of Lord Jowitt, "inconsistent with the political conception which is embodied in the British commonwealth of nations".
Surely I need no better authority than the privy council itself for the argument that our present status as a sovereign member of the British commonwealth demands the action which is proposed in this bill.
Before turning to the other point which concerns our relationship in the united nations, let me deal for a moment with the arguments which might be, and undoubtedly will be, advanced against this measure. There is the contention that it would destroy the preroga-

tive of His Majesty. I think we can dismiss this argument as invalid in view of the long standing and adopted British constitutional conception. It is unthinkable that His Majesty could act without the advice of the privy council, and it has been held on numerous occasions that the privy council is, in fact, an appellate court of law.
In the case of the British Coal Corporation versus The King, 1935, 3 D.L.R., 401, the privy council itself says this:
It is clear that the committee is regarded in the act as a judicial body or court, though all it e.an do is to report or recommend to His Majesty in Council by whom alone the order in council which is made to give effect to the report of the committee is made. But according to constitutional convention it is unknown and unthinkable that His Majesty in Council should not give effect to the report of the judicial committee who are thus in truth an appellate court of law, to which, by the statute of 1833 all appeals within their purview are referred.
It is clear, therefore, that in passing this bill we are not in the slightest degree interfering with any supposedly existing prerogative of His Majesty. We are simply substituting one final ultimate appeal court of our own for another which is not our own, and about the composition, jurisdiction and powers of which we have no voice whatsoever.
In anticipating arguments in opposition to the bill of last session I mentioned, and I disagreed then with the position taken by some people, that the privy council should be retained as the final court of appeal because it would be a neutral or more impartial tribunal to adjudicate upon controversies involving the interpretation of our constitution, the British North America Act. I find that this sort of argument still forms the main source of opposition to a measure such as the one before the house at the moment.
I also find the argument advanced that we might abolish all appeals to the privy council except cases which involve a constitutional question. With that I disagree entirely. In the first place, I would say that such arguments are not very complimentary to Canadian judges who are as good judges as any in the British empire. In the second place, I shall contend that Canadian judges who have lived here all their lives, who are conversant with Canadian life, Canadian habits, and who know Canadian social, economic and industrial conditions are in a much better position to interpret our constitution in the light of ever-changing circumstances in this country of ours. You see, I do not regard our constitution as a dry, inflexible law or statute, and although I will admit that it needs to be changed in some places, I think the framers of this law

Supreme Court Act Amendment
and its sponsors, the fathers of confederation, did very well, and when they built this constitution I think they had the future in mind.
I said once before in this parliament, and I should like to emphasize again, that the fathers of confederation were out to create a unified nation. Canadian unity is, in my opinion, the cornerstone of the British North America Act, and it is in that light that its various provisions should be interpreted. I think we can safely leave that interpretation to Canadian judges. There is no question that, as time passes, conditions will arise through the natural progress which we are bound to make, which will require the interpretation of the British North America Act in the light of the emergence of such new conditions, which conditions will be bound to be subject to dispute as to where the jurisdiction rests to legislate with respect to such new circumstances. I believe that such disputes will in future be decided more or less upon the basis of the recent privy council decision in respect of the Canada Temperance Act case, which says that parliament has jurisdiction, under the peace, order and good government clause, on any subject that, by its inherent nature, is of national importance. I have an idea that future constitutional disputes will revolve about that question, and I believe that Canadian judges will be in a better position to adjudicate upon such a point, namely, as to what is a subject which, by its inherent nature, is of national importance, and what, on the other hand, is a matter of merely provincial or local concern.
These judges, as Canadians, will have been part and parcel of this national progress. They will understand better the causes of changing conditions, and for these reasons I maintain that Canadian judges are in a better position than the learned law lords of the privy council in interpreting the Canadian constitution as a flexible, progressive statute, which, as Lord Sanke.v once said, "was a live tree capable of growth and expansion within its natural limits."
The only hon. member who was able to take part in the debate last year was the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who opposed the passing of the measure in no uncertain terms, basing his argument mainly, as I understood him, upon the supposition that the privy council has been the great defender of the rights of minorities of this country, and likewise that the provinces were not favourable to this bill because the privy council was the guardian of provincial rights. I think it is, to say the least, incongruous to argue in this manner, because the judges of
our supreme court come from different provinces and they understand, better than anyone, provincial rights or the rights of minorities.
I have not taken any census of the numerous decisions rendered by the privy council upon constitutional questions since confederation. but I venture to say that the decisions rendered against the provinces and favourable to the dominion are more numerous than decisions rendered the other way. In any event, however, the argument is invalid. If you say that the privy council has been the guardian of provincial rights you suggest that that body has favoured the provinces as against the dominion, and that sounds to me rather like a reflection on them, which is certainly unjustified. Our courts of law bestow no favours.
As to the privy council being a great defender of the rights of minorities, I may say that the records of the decisions of the privy council with regard to minority rights would certainly not bear out that this is a fact. If you refer to that most excellent book of Doctor Maurice Olliver on "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty", you will see the leading cases on minority rights cited, which appear to be proof of the fact that most cases show that the people who claimed certain rights as minorities were told by the privy council that they did not have any such rights.
I have also heard it argued of late that we should retain the appeals to the privy council because the decisions may form a. valuable part of our jurisprudence based upon English common law. That, of course, would not be true if applied to the civil law of the province of Quebec. But even if we did abolish appeals to the privy council, any judgments which they might render in the future would still be valuable, as in our courts we look with great respect upon the judgments of British courts, although these judgments may not be binding in our courts. Therefore I maintain that there is no argument on that score either.
I mentioned in my opening remarks a few moments ago that I maintained as a second point that the retention of the privy council as a Canadian court of appeal was inconsistent with our status as a member of the united nations. The charter of the united nations on membership qualifications states that we must be able and willing under our own laws to enforce and carry out the obligations which we undertake when we become a member of that great organization. I maintain that, by retaining the privy council as the final court of appeal, we offend against that qualification, because it would not be a court of our own

Supreme Court Act Amendment
making which might have the final word with respect to our obligations as a member of the united nations.
For instance, there is the act which we passed last year, being chapter 69, to provide for privileges and immunities in respect of the united nations and related international organizations. That ant contains as a schedule the convention on the privileges and immunities of the united nations. It is quite possible that there might be some legal controversy as to the interpretation of the act or of the convention which forms part of it. As a matter of fact, article 1 states:
The united nations shall possess juridical personality. It shall have the capacity:
(a)	to contract;
(b)	to acquire and dispose of immovable and movable property;
(c)	to institute legal proceedings.
It has that authority to institute legal proceedings within our jurisdiction; that is, within Canada. Section 34 of the convention which is ratified and adopted by chapter 69 of the 1947 statutes reads as follows:
It is understood that, when an instrument of accession is deposited on behalf of any member, the member will be in a position under its own law to give effect to the terms of this convention.
I emphasize the language used in that article, namely, "under its own laws." Our judicial system is established by law, but that system includes the highest court of appeal, which is not constituted under our own laws. Therefore I would argue that we offend against the convention adopted by this statute because we are not in a position under our own laws to give effect to the terms of the convention.
The sections of the statute just quoted and the articles of the convention itself suggest that there may be legal proceedings for their enforcement, instituted even by the united nations itself. All of this might be subject to appeal to the privy council, and we might find ourselves in what I believe would be an embarrassing position if the privy council, a court which is not our own, should tell us what our duties and obligations were in connection with a relationship into which we had entered as a sovereign state.
Then there is chapter 46 of the statutes of 1947, the United Nations Act. This act provides that if the security council decides upon a measure, including the interruption of economic relations, the governor in council may make orders and regulations enabling such measures to be effectively applied. The act means that if the security council requires us

to do so we have to apply economic sanctions or any other sanction short of war against an offending member of the united nations. If we pass regulations in respect thereof I can imagine litigation arising from such regulations, such as the numerous prosecutions which occurred under the War Measures Act. I can imagine a possible appeal to the privy council and that body telling Canada, a sovereign nation of the united nations, what our duties are with respect to the obligations we have entered into.
Apart from' our status as a member of the united nations, there is our general relationship as a sovereign state to the other nations of the world. For instance, take the case of the Polish art treasures about which there might be a lawsuit which would command headlines on the front pages of the daily press. However innocent and well meant were the actions of the dominion and Quebec governments in this mix-up, they might very easily become an important feature in such a lawsuit. Imagine the possibility of the privy council having to adjudicate upon that matter in the light of the acts of the dominion or the province concerned!
I think it is intolerable to contemplate that Canada as a sovereign state, wThich it is in fact whether we like it or not, should submit in a case such as this to the judgment of a court which is not our own. To me the retention of the privy council as the final court of appeal is incompatible with our membership as a sovereign state in the united nations. I commend this bill to the favourable consideration of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the time
reserved for public bills is very limited, my remarks will be rather brief.
The bill proposes to abolish appeals to the judicial committee of the privy council.
Since the enactment of the Statute of Westminster by the imperial parliament, on December 11, 1931, which recognized Canada's sovereignty this matter has been discussed at the sessions of 1937, 1938 and particularly that of 1939, when the then Minister of Justice. Mr. Ernest Lapointe, unreservedly approved a similar bill introduced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. James, Mr. Cahan.
However, passage of the bill was delayed until such time as the government could obtain the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada and of the privy council regarding the power of parliament to legislate in that matter.
Since it was decided by the supreme court, in 1940, and by the privy council, in January 1947, that the dominion parliament had the

Supreme Court Act Amendment
power to abolish appeals to the judicial committee of the privy council, we have reason to wonder why the government did not introduce, in 1947, a bill implementing those decisions. I hope that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who asserted that he favoured the abolition of those appeals, when he was chairman of the Canadian Bar Association, will facilitate the passage of this bill which may otherwise meet with the same fate as the one introduced last year by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke).
We have every reason for acting without delay. First, our present position is incompatible with our status of sovereign nation. Canada is a free and sovereign country and is recognized as such by other nations. Canada is a member of the United Nations Organization, based on the principle of the equal sovereignty of all its members, and even holds a seat in the security council. Yet, for the administration of justice, one of the most important functions in a really free and autonomous country, Canada depends on a foreign court which operates outside our borders.
Under such circumstances, what is meant by equal status and full autonomy? What is understood by the Statute of Westminster? Our prestige among nations is at stake unless we eliminate as soon as possible this ancient vestige of our colonial status which hinders our judicial autonomy and fosters among us an inferiority complex.
In so far as Canadian courts feel bound by decisions of the privy council which, in effect, are akin to enactments, this state of ihings interferes with our legislative autonomy.
In his book on Responsible Government in the Colonies, Keith says at page 1102:
It is idle to deny that the taking of appeals to the privy council is a mark of inferior status and partial servility . . . The maintenance of the present position is just and proper so long as the dominions desire to remain dependencies.
Moreover, it is insulting to our judicial body and humiliating to the entire Canadian population to maintain this right of appeal. It implies that we have not among us people sufficiently enlightened, sufficiently intelligent, to interpret our laws and statutes and that we must ask a foreign court for an ultimate decision in matters at issue. We are able to enact our laws but unable to interpret them.
Would anyone claim, for instance, that in a matter of civil law, a foreign judge with little or no knowledge of our Quebec civil code would be more likely to safeguard the interests of the
citizen than our own judges with their lifelong experience? Here also one may not forget that their lord justices seeing no difference between the Quebec civil code and the common law, as they have often stated, have been too prone to abide by the precedents of the English courts.
Some claim that the privy council is the guardian of minority rights. In the light of experience, far from being so, this claim is but a myth as was stated by the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe. Were this not sufficient, I could remind hon. members of the judgments rendered in the cases of the school laws of New Brunswick, in 1871, of Manitoba (Barrett v. Winnipeg) in 1892, of the Ontario Regulation No. XVII, and in the case Despatie-Tremblay. Without any exception, the judgments of their lordships were against the claims of the minority. Moreover, the privy council is more a political than a judicial body. As was stated in this house by Mr. Cahan, in 1937:
Many of its active members are at the same time members of a legislative division of the British parliament. The Lord Chief Justice is a member of the government of the United Kingdom and no report of the judicial committee can be binding unless approved by an order of the British privy council.
This accounts for certain decisions such as that which, in 1927, granted Newfoundland a portion of Labrador peninsula which until then had been part of the province of Quebec.
Moreover, such appeals to the privy council wreak an injustice upon people of slender means, because they are too costly. After all, it is within the reach only of great corporations and wealthy people. Let the hon. members imagine the costs of taking a case to London, and the predicament of the Canadian citizen of limited means who faces the threat of an appeal to the privy council, after winning his case in a Canadian court. Unable to meet the costs of such an appeal, he agrees to some more or less advantageous settlement, which means that powerful companies have used the outside tribunal as an instrument of intimidation.
What of the multiplicity of appeal jurisdictions whose very numbers increase judicial costs and hamper the administration of justice? In our judicial system, there are three appeal courts, including the privy council, whereas two appeal jurisdictions within Canada, namely the Court of King's Bench and the Supreme Court of Canada, are amply sufficient. As far as I know, that number is not exceeded in other countries.

Supreme Court Act Amendment
As an example of the delay caused by this third appeal to the privy council, there is the Despatie-Tremblay case, first heard in the province of Quebec Superior Court on June 26, 1911, then carried to the privy council where it was first heard in 1914 and finally settled on February 11, 1921, after a second hearing, that is ten years after the decision in the first instance.
I remember a saying of a former justice of the Court- of King's Bench, Sir Horace Archambault:
Justice which is not expeditious is not justice.
Let us therefore put an end to these injustices and rid ourselves of this last vestige of colonialism.
We are concerned today with abolishing appeals to the privy council, but I believe it would be proper to complete this legislation by regulating the working of the Supreme Court.
In any case involving civil law or civil procedure, the decision of the provincial court of appeals should be final, and the right of appeal to the Supreme Court abolished. Alternatively, it should be decided that the cases from Quebec should be heard by five judges, including three from Quebec, and the cases from the other provinces by at least three judges from such other provinces.
In constitutional cases a special court could be set up. including the judges from the Supreme Court and the chief justice from every province.
But let us begin by abolishing appeals to the privy council.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH APPEALS TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke), Mr. Speaker, on having introduced again this year a bill to abolish appeals to the privy council. He said tonight that this was the next logical step in the establishment of Canada's sovereignty.
I am in perfect agreement not only with what he said on that point but generally with all the reasons he gave, both tonight and last year, in favour of the abolition of the right of appeal to the privy council.
( Translation):
May I also congratulate the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) for his truly Canadian stand on this subject? After his speech, there can be no doubt in our minds about his genuine Canadian spirit. Once more I commend him for it.

Several reasons have been brought forward in the two speeches which I have just mentioned, as well as in others made on previous occasions, for tne elimination of appeals to the privy council. Outstanding remarks have been made especially by the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe and by the hon. Mr. Cahan. The argument presented by Mr. Maurice Ollivier, in his book, is consistent, perfectly established and most convincing. While thus reminding the hon. members of outstanding contributions on the subject, I do not intend' to repeat tonight in my own words all arguments previously adduced.
As was stated last year by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke), the right of our Canadian parliament to do away with appeals to the privy council has been definitely established by the privy council itself. All we have now to discuss is the advisability' of a bill such as this.
Before dealing with this matter, I should like as briefly as possible to call the attention of the house to the following point. Bill No. 5 would do away with all appeals to the privy council and even with the appeals to the royal prerogative, commonly known as appeals to the throne. Therefore, no Canadian citizen would have the right to appeal to the King in the case of certain grievances for which no remedy may be sought from other jurisdictions.
Though I would not wish to give a final opinion on this matter, I am inclined to believe that on this score serious objection could be had to the bill as now drafted It is not inconceivable that serious trouble might arise from the final decision of a court due to gross injustices which would be without remedy after the elimination of these appeals to the throne. Of course, this objectionable feature does not challenge the principle of the bill but it might properly be the subject matter of an amendment in committee. I wonder if it would not be better to amend the bill so as to allow appeals to the Governor General who would act on the advice given to him by the Supreme Court after having heard all parties concerned, except of course in cases already dealt with by that court. I am not in a position to express a definite opinion on the matter, but no doubt that many hon. members have had enough experience in legal matters and are conversant enough with those questions to put forth useful and interesting opinions.

Supreme Court Act Amendment
I repeat, however, that there is not the slightest doubt in my mind about the principle of the bill, which I entirely approve.
The judicial committee of the privy council was empowered by chapters 3 and 4, William IV, to hear any appeal from His Majesty's colonies. Previously, the appeals from the colonies were heard by His Majesty in council. The said committee was established to hear appeals from the colonies, but not appeals from judgments brought down in England and Scotland.
After the hearing, the judicial committee of the privy council submits a report to the King, stating the 'easons which have motivated the lords' decision, advising His Majesty to give effect to their recommendation. The report is then referred to the King in council for the United Kingdom, and not for Canada, and is approved. An order in council is then passed, quoting the report verbatim. The decision then becomes the King's judgment.
From the above, it should be remembered that the judgments of the privy council are, in fact, only judgments of the King and his council for the United Kingdom-that is of the British government-judgments which are rendered upon the recommendation of the lords, who are members of the judicial committee of the privy council. In its very essence, this court is of a colonial order. That, to my mind, is the main reason why Canada can no longer allow decisions of our courts to be appealed to the privy council.

It has been suggested, especially by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Laprairie, that constitutional cases between the federal government and the provinces be heard both by the justices of the supreme court and by the chief justices of the various provinces, in the capacity of ad hoc supreme court justices. On the other hand, before we endorse the bill introduced by the hon. member for Kindersley, I think we should not wait until the suggestion I have just mentioned or some other proposal along the same lines, is carried out. To my mind it is so urgent for a sovereign nation like Canada to remove the colonial humiliation implied by the existence of the right of appeal to the privy council that the passing of this bill should not be further delayed.

In some respects, the British North America Act is certainly inconsistent with the present sovereign status of this country.

Mr. Chairman, may I first of all make some references to these estimates for the Department of Agriculture. We have read and heard about many reports in which the Department of Finance has boasted of a surplus of well over $750 million in the past fiscal year. Bearing that fact in mind, I note that, while the estimates for the fiscal year 1947-48 amounted to $63,185,158.37, the amount for the fiscal year 1948-49 is only $41,822,602, showing a decrease, in the present year, of $21,362,556.37. That is an enlightening comparison in view of the greatest surplus in history about which the government as a whole
Supply-Agriculture

are boasting. I think there is too heavy a decrease in the estimated expenditures for the Department of Agriculture for the coming year. I know that many of us are asking for decreases in governmental expenditure, but I do not think that under present conditions there should be a decrease in this department. Our present per capita expenditure on Canadian agriculture is very much less than that of the United States. In the United States last year their expenditure on agriculture was, I understand, $1,247 million. Our population is approximately one-twelfth of theirs, and to be on the same footing we should be spending well over $100 million on agriculture this year.
As has often been pointed out, our own Canadian government has placed an embargo against beef cattle going to the United States. That was imposed in 1942 and still exists, and the beef producers of the west and their association are very much concerned lest they lose that natural market of theirs in the future. They have recently briefed the Prime Minister about it, also the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance.
This government has also placed embargoes against other agricultural products entering the United States. When you think of those embargoes and then consider that, according to the press, a statement was issued by the Minister of Agriculture the other day that we now have 48 per cent more meat in storage in this country today than we had a year ago-

I know the hon. member would not want to leave on the record a statement which is not correct. I am not criticizing him for putting it on, because the statement did come over the radio on Sunday morning that we had 48 per cent more meat in storage than we had a year ago. I immediately got in touch with those who put the statement on and it did not go out over the radio again or appear in the press. The report was inaccurate.
I am glad to hear that. Can the minister tell us what the correct figure is?

I can get the exact figures but it was not anything like that. The 48 per cent increase was the amount of bacon hogs which were delivered in January of this year as compared with January of a year ago.
Can the minister say Where the radio and the press got their information?

No. It was just a wrong
impression that a reporter got from a statement which was made.

I am glad to have the minister's correction, because the statement received publicity all across Canada. On the other hand I believe there is a lot of meat in storage and we should be glad to have the exact figures on that.
With respect to feed grain, I understand that there is a much greater quantity on hand today than there has been for many years. I understand from a report that there is a surplus of 10,000,000 bushels of barley. The minister will correct me if the report was inaccurate.

I think the statement was made on the radio that there was a surplus of 10.000,000 bushels of barley that was to be sold outside Canada, but the actual statement which the reporter said he made was that there were 5,000,000 bushels of barley and 5,000,000 bushels of oats, the two making 10,000,000 bushels, which was likely to be exported.

I am glad to have that correction. We should like to have the exact figures, because I understand that there is a surplus of feed in Canada at this time as well as of meat. There is consternation among the coarse grain producers in western Canada, especially those who marketed their grain between August 1 last fall and the date of lifting the ceiling. The minister has said on several occasions that an adjustment would be made, but it is now seven months since the ceiling was taken off and many producers who sold their grain during that period are anxious to know when the adjustment will be made. It seems to me that they ought to be told, because at present confusion exists. There was a federal-provincial conference last fall and a plan was issued for the guidance of the farmers this year; nevertheless considerable confusion exists among western farmers as to what they should plant at this season of the year.
A question that is uppermost in my mind and in the minds of many people who have spoken to me is, what prospect have Canadian producers of marketing agricultural products this year through the Marshall plan? I believe that plan has been approved by the United States authorities, and I would assume that our Canadian authorities have been negotiating with United States officials. If no agreement has actually been signed as yet, perhaps the minister could give us some idea of what our agricul-

Supply-Agriculture
tural producers might reasonably expect to market through the Marshall plan. This information would be very useful to those who are about to proceed with their planting operations at this time of year.
If the minister would make a fairly full statement at this time I think it would tend to shorten the debate and save a lot of questions, and certainly it would facilitate the passage of his estimates.
Would it be possible for the minister and his assistants to move nearer the agricultural centre of gravity in this house?
I shall be glad to do so.

Now that we have the Minister of Agriculture among the farmers, we can get down to business. I agree with the hon. member for Souris that it certainly needs a little bit of explaining why there should be such a large decrease in the estimated expenditures for agriculture for the coming year. The decrease would seem to indicate that the government are satisfied that we have as efficient agricultural production as it is possible to have in this country, and that we have also a growing agricultural production in Canada. Neither is the case, if we take the government's own publications as our authority. For instance, 28 per cent of the farms in Canada today are subsistence farms.
The definition which I am using of a subsistence farm is one that produces less for sale than is consumed on the farm itself. There is a tremendous variation between different parts of Canada in the number of subsistence farms. Alberta has the lowest percentage, with 15 per cent; Saskatchewan, 16 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 40 per cent, and New Brunswick, 51 per cent. Anyone who has visited Prince Edward Island knows that province has a soil which is as productive as that of any other province in the dominion. Yet 40 per cent of the farms, to use the definition that I have given, are on a subsistence level. The 28 per cent of the farms of Canada that are on a subsistence level produced less than 10 per cent of the total marketed' agricultural production of Canada; while 10 per cent of the most productive farms in the country produced over 30 per cent of the marketed agricultural produce of Canada. This indicates that there is need of a great deal of extension work, both in the federal Department of Agriculture and in the provincial departments of agriculture. There should not be such a variation 5849-215i
in the production capacities of our farms as is indicated by these figures.
Probably we have a greater investment in agriculture in Canada than we have in any other industry. I believe that the investment in agriculture in this country should be protected in every possible way. We protect our investment in other great industries. Take our railways. When they show a deficit we are prepared to give them a 21 per cent increase in freight rates to protect their investment. Take our packing industry. The evidence given before a committee of the house would indicate that the capital invested in our packing industry is amply protected in Canada. The figures given there show that an investment of $2,500,000 made by Canada Packers when that company was formed some twenty years ago has today grown into some $86,000,000 without the investment of another cent by the company.
They paid off all their indebtedness in various forms, such as bonds which they had to issue during the early years of the amalgamation of the companies which went into Canada Packers. They built up millions of dollars of reserves in their reserve accounts. If the agricultural industry which has supplied most of the capital for this increase in the investment in these various industries, in our railways, in our packing industries, is not protected as it should be, then the drop in the expenditures indicated in the estimates for this year cannot be justified.
We should have certain objectives for our agricultural industry in this country. The first objective should, as I say, be to produce efficiently for optimum nutrition for all our people, and to produce all the possible raw materials for industry that industry might need from agriculture. Second, to establish for all workers in agriculture a standard of living comparable with that provided in the better organized urban industries, especially in relation to housing, educational opportunities and facilities in health and general culture. Third, to produce, over and1 above domestic needs, the maximum amount of agricultural commodities for export. If we had an agricultural policy in Canada which would meet these three requirements, then we would be much better off in the agricultural industry than we are today.
Let us see how we are meeting these three requirements: first, to produce efficiently the food necessary for nutrition in this country and to supply the export markets. We find strangely today that in agriculture, with some
100,000	young people returning from the
Supply-Agriculture

armed forces and entering that industry, our production is decreasing. I hold in my hand a current review of agricultural conditions in Canada for February, 1948. This indicates that inspected slaughterings of cattle during 1947 amounted to 1-3 million head, a decline of 22 per cent from 1946. There was a 30 per cent decline in western Canada and a 10 per cent drop in eastern Canada.
Take hogs. During 1947, 4,765,000 hogs were marketed in Canada, a slight increase over
4,465,000	marketed in 1946. However, in western Canada there was a 12 per cent decline, while in eastern Canada there was a 20 per cent increase.
I want to say something with regard to the policy of the government which has, during the last three years, practically wiped out the hog industry in western Canada. If there is one place where hogs can be produced efficiently and at the lowest cost it is in western Canada, where the grain for feeding is grown; yet we find that the policy of the government since almost the beginning of the war has been such as to re-direct the production of hogs in Canada from the west to the east. I have no objection to the increasing of hog production in eastern Canada to the maximum amount necessary to make good use of all the byproducts of the dairy industry that can be fed efficiently in eastern Canada. But when we pay the subsidy on coarse grains that we are paying in shipping these grains from western Canada to eastern Canada, and these grains are used for the production of hogs in eastern Canada, then I do not see why the government should continue that policy. That policy is all right so long as these grains are used to increase the dairy industry in eastern Canada. Probably the dairy industry needs that subsidy. But when we find large quantities of this grain being used for the production of hogs in eastern Canada and, on the other hand, the production of hogs in western Canada declining where, by all measures of efficiency, the production should be increasing, then I think it is a wrong policy. The government should re-direct this policy.
We want to see some diversification in western Canada in the agricultural industry, and it seems to me that the production of hogs and poultry are two particular agricultural products which we can increase in that area of Canada, and produce more efficiently than they can be produced in any other part of the dominion.
Let us take a look at dairy products. Milk production in 1947 recovered from the decline of 1946. The production in 1947 of 17-2 billion pounds shows an increase of 1-6 per

cent, but on the other hand we have a decline of 19-4 per cent in the production of cheese, and a somewhat similar decline in the production of certain other dairy products. I am convinced that, through the Department of Agriculture, we should have some program which will increase our production of agricultural products in Canada.
My second requirement was to establish for all workers in agriculture a standard of living comparable with that provided in the better organized urban industries, especially in relation to housing, educational opportunities and facilities in health and general culture. What is the picture in Canada with regard to facilities which we have on our farms? I hold in my hand the figures which were prepared by the Ontario government, "A Conspectus of the Province of Ontario", prepared by the Ontario bureau of statistics and the research section of the department of the provincial treasurer. This paints a pretty dark picture of the conditions that we find on farms in Canada today. Even in Ontario, which is probably the best agricultural province, the one in which they have the most facilities-
The best province all round.

I do not agree with that, although, due to its particular situation close to the large manufacturing centres, the agricultural industry in this province is in a more favourable position than that in any other part of the dominion. I think it will be agreed that even in good old Ontario conditions are not just as good as they might be.
For instance, over 50,000 Ontario farmers have no automobiles. We do better than that in western Canada. Over 160,000 Ontario farmers have no motor trucks, and over 140,000 have no tractors. Over 145,000 farm, homes in Ontario have no means of refrigeration and over 160,000 farm homes in Ontario have no vacuum cleaners. Over 60,000 homes in Ontario have no radios and over 125,000 farm homes have no running water. Over 85,000 farm homes in Ontario have no telephones and over
130,000	are still heated by stoves, not having furnaces. Over 160,000 Ontario farm homes still have outside toilets and over 160,000 farm homes have no bath or shower equipment.
What are you reading from.

It is a "Conspectus of the Province of Ontario," prepared by the Ontario bureau of statistics and the research section of the department of the provincial treasurer. This table gives the percentages for 1941 in all provinces.

I do not think many of these facilities would be put in Ontario farm homes during the war, especially if you were doing your part in the war effort. I would ask the permission of the committee to place on the record the figures for all the provinces. I admit that Ontario is the best even with its needs.

On a point of order, this request is antiquated and is out of date; it is not a legal request because the table is dated 1941 and this is the year of grace 1948. Even though Ontario had the best record in 1941, it would have a better record in 1948. Why clutter up the record with 1941 figures?

Then I shall simply have to give the figures for the other provinces. I know the Minister of Agriculture is anxious to get his estimates through but it will be quite easy to put the figures for the other provinces on the record. In Prince Edward Island 29 per cent of farm homes and buildings need external repairs. Only nine per cent of the homes have inside running water and only six per cent have electric lighting. Only 10 per cent are heated by furnaces and only 12 per cent have either mechanical or ice refrigeration. Fifty-four per cent of the homes have radios, 18 per cent have telephones but only two per cent have vacuum cleaners. Only 30 per cent of the farmers have automobiles.
In Saskatchewan 47 per cent of the farm homes and buildings need repairs. It will be realized that this is before the C.C.F. government came into pow'er in Saskatchewan. Only one per cent of the homes have running water, while only five per cent have electric lighting. Only 12 per cent have furnace heating and only six per cent have mechanical or ice refrigeration. Seventy-two per cent of the homes have radios, while 33 per cent have telephones. Only one per cent have vacuum cleaners and 46 per cent have automobiles.
But they have a C.C.F. government and they would not want anything more!

If the people in Ontario had percentages as low as that they probably would be wise enough to get a C.C.F. government to improve conditions here.
In Quebec 40 per cent of the farm homes need repairs and only 25 per cent have running water. Only 24 per cent have electric lighting and only 10 per cent have furnace heating. Only 14 per cent have refrigeration, while 36 per cent have radios. Sixteen per cent of the homes have telephones but only one per cent have vacuum cleaners. Sixteen per cent have automobiles.
I think these figures are sufficient to indicate the position of the farming industry today. Apparently my hon. friends in the Conservative party are not much interested in conditions on our farms today. They seem to be more interested when we are dealing with the packing industry. We do not have as many interjections when we are talking along those lines as we have when we are talking about the facilities in the farm homes of Canada. When you are referring to any other financial interest in Canada you do not have the interruptions you have when you talk about the position of agriculture. If my hon. friends would get up and defend agriculture they would be doing more good, instead of interrupting as they are.

Come down to our
province and see.
How many Tory members are there in Saskatchewan?
How many C.C.F. members are there in Ontario?

speechtext: I must ask hon. members to permit the hon. member to make his speech.
Just playing politics.
The hon. member for Peel talks about playing politics, but I do not know of any other hon. member in this house who does that more consistently than he.
Or more successfully.
I am not playing politics; I am just stating the position of agriculture in this country today.
Seven years ago.

The sooner we recognize that position the sooner we shall get legislation in this house that will be favourable toward agriculture and give agriculture in this country the position which it should have as the first industry and one of the most important in the country.

That will not get one
vote for Mr. Jolliffe in Ontario.

At least the hon. member might come into the chamber to make his
Supply-Agriculture

interjections, and on this first item in agriculture he might attempt to do something for the farmer in Peel county which he represents. I admit that that is one of the best agricultural counties in Ontario.
If the agricultural industry in Canada were given an equal opportunity with other industries, I believe we should find that they would make a maximum contribution toward the welfare of this country, not only in raising our nutritional standards but in supplying more foods for export to other countries which need them at the present time.
The position in the world today with respect to food is serious. It is so serious that, because of discontent caused by malnutrition, we find growing throughout the world communism and a great many other things which we do not like and which we should like to see stopped. One of the best ways in which we can stop the growth of communism or any other ism is by the abundant production of food and the proper distribution of it throughout the world. I think the objective of agriculture in this country should be: first, the supplying of the nutritional needs of our own country, and then the production of the maximum amount of food for export to those countries which today need that food.

It would appear that the question of agriculture is a little bit distasteful to some of the members of the house tonight; but I do not know of any group who can enjoy the products of the farm better than some of those who have been butting in on the speaker who has just taken his seat. While I am one who enjoys his eats just about as well as anybody else, I think the question of agriculture is of sufficient importance that we should give it the consideration to which it is entitled, and should give it its proper place in the Canadian economy.
I feel that agriculture, as it has been in the past and as it is now, will continue in the future to be the basic industry of Canada. In the past, agriculture has not had its proper share of the national income. The farmers on the land and those working for them have had a poorer standard of living than has any other occupational group in Canada that I can think of. I know that from personal experience, because I have been farming for more than thirty years and should know a little bit about it. I think also that every other profession in Canada is dependent, either directly or indirectly, upon agriculture. For that reason, I consider that all of us, whether we live on a farm, in a town or in a city, should give agriculture the attention to which it is entitled.

I am sorry to see that the Minister of Agriculture has agreed to have the estimates for his department cut by about one-third this year. There is perhaps some excuse for it. Perhaps the autocratic treasury board would not allow him any more money. But I feel that he and we should protest against the cut in the estimates.
While many people today consider that agriculture is really prosperous, I could give an entirely different picture. If those people to whom I have referred took the trouble to investigate the real position of agriculture today, they would find that it is not nearly as prosperous as some people would lead us to believe. While the farmers have today reduced their debt much below what it was at the time war broke out, I am quite satisfied that if the farmers were to put their buildings and their machinery in as good shape as those things were in 1939, there would not be so much money for paying off debts as some people imagine. The farmers of this country have not been able, during the past seven or eight years, to buy the machinery they require. For that reason they have been compelled to produce with dilapidated machinery such as tractors and other implements. Their buildings have gone down in condition, and it will take many thousands of dollars to bring them up to the state of repair at which they were at the time war broke out.
Again I feel that while we have accepted, and are still accepting, prices below those to which we are entitled, we have not yet done anything in fact about stabilizing the agricultural industry in the years to come. That is one of the main things about which we should be concerned at the present time. Again, while the price of butter has gone up a little bit, and there is a battle on by some people who apparently are interested in the production and sale of margarine in Canada, I feel that butter is not selling at a higher price than that at which it should be selling. But because, during the depression years and during the early years of the war, butter sold at a low price, many people believe that it should continue to be sold at that low price, even although the wages of all the workers in Canada and the incomes of other people as well have increased considerably during the past seven or eight years.
I do not intend to say much more in this connection, but I consider that we should all work toward a policy of stabilization which will give agriculture the place to which it is entitled in Canada; because, if we have not a successful agriculture, we cannot have

Supply-Agriculture
success in other parts of Canada. We were told in 1938 that agriculture in the prairie provinces absorbed 69 per cent of the farm implements that were manufactured in central Canada. If we are to be able in the future to purchase our share of the farm implements and other things that are manufactured in central Canada, then we must see to it, whether we live on the land or not, that we are given an agricultural policy which will guarantee prosperity on the farms in all parts of Canada.

One representative from each of the three groups opposite has spoken with regard to the estimates, and probably I should deal with the general criticisms that are made before we go farther. It has been pointed out that there has been a decrease in the estimates, in the figures as shown. The summary is on page 7 of the main estimates. The ordinary expenditures of the department are in round figures, $18,600,000 this year. They were $17,000,000 last year. So that under ordinary expenditures there is an increase of $1,579,000. Then, on the specials, there is $8,865,000 this year and there was $15,433,000 last year, or a decrease of $6,567,000. Then, under demobilization and reconversion there is $14,298,000 this year and there was $30,672,000 last year, or a decrease of $16,374,000. The figures show a total for 1948-49 of $41,810,000 as compared with $63,173,000 last year, or a decrease, as has been indicated, of $21,362,000.
While it is true that there has been a considerable decrease, it will be noted that there is not a decrease in the items that were voted prior to the war. There is a marked increase in the ordinary expenditures under agriculture, and the specials are of such a nature as to indicate that this is not unexpected. They are all noted in the items that are voted. There is a reduction of $7,773,000. The first item is to authorize and provide for the payment of subsidies on oats and barley used to feed livestock; and since those subsidies have been removed and are now part of the price of the grain, that figure is down by $6,000,000. Next is prairie farm rehabilitation and water storage, which is down $1. Then comes the amount required to recoup the agricultural prices support account to cover the net operating loss of the agricultural prices support board, $171,053. That, of course, was an amount taken out last year in order to cover certain items for which we could not secure the money elsewhere. The next item is to authorize and provide for the payment of subsidies on oats and barley used as feed for livestock under vote 715, $1,600,000; and to provide for a grant to the Federated Women's Institute of Canada, $2,000. It will be noted that $7,600,000 out of the $7,773,000 is
in connection with reduced subsidies on feed grain, so that no further explanation is required to indicate the reason for the reduction.
Then, under demobilization and reconversion there is an item covering the appropriation not required for 1948-49, $6,035,625. This is made up as follows. Under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the agricultural board, $2,030,000; agricultural supplies board, $42,700; to encourage the production of essential supplies, $102,250; food administrator, including freight assistance on western feed grains, $21,000,000 voted for 1947-48, less $18,000,000 only required for 1947-48, leaving a balance of $3,036,875 not required. Then there is the vote for the fertilizers and pesticides administrator, including subsidies on lime and bulk purchasing of fertilizer chemicals, $618,300, and for the seeds administrator, $205,000. It will be noted that the greater part of the reduction is $3,036,000 on freights paid on western grain; but as a matter of fact, since these estimates were prepared, I have announced that we will continue the freight payments for- the year 1948-49, which will mean that, instead of a reduction, the sum of $16,000,000 will have to be added to this item.
That pretty well takes care of the reduction we have been talking about. Some $16,000,000 additional will be required in order to continue to pay the freight, since in these estimates we have provision for the payment of freight only until August 1 next, an amount of about $7,000,000. We shall require over $23,000,000, however, to pay the freight from Fort William east on an amount of grain similar to what was shipped last year, though we estimate that the amount of grain will be greater this year, the chief reason for the increase being the 21 per cent freight rate increase. Therefore we anticipate that the total this year will be $23,000,000 instead of the $18,000,000 last year. I should have said, of course, that we pay the freight not only from Fort William east but also on grain moving west from Calgary and Edmonton to British Columbia. So that our estimates for this year will not be very much below the figures of last year.
I believe that is sufficient to indicate that there is very little difference, and where any difference does exist it is entirely a matter of doing away with some of the expenditures we were making during the war, but which are not now considered necessary. In saying that, I might emphasize that this is quite a different picture from that of some thirteen years ago. Then the expenditures on agriculture had been gradually reduced until they were at a very low level, and from that time up to the present

they have greatly increased. I remember attending a meeting in the city of Toronto after I had been minister for one or two years. One of the daily newspapers devoted a whole page to an attack upon myself, in which they asked me to explain at a public meeting why I should have spent $20,000,000 in the Department of Agriculture. Tonight I am being criticized, by some of the same people who were criticizing an expenditure of $20,000,000, for spending only something over $40,000,000 this year.
No, it is not the same people.
I am not very much concerned about the criticism at either time. The expenditures have been gradually increasing on matters considered essential to agriculture.
Who were the people? Not those who are here tonight.

Well, in any event they represent some of the same people; I think most of the Toronto seats are represented over on that side of the house. I have just been handed the exact figures of the expenditures of this department from that time. Well, snow does a lot of good sometimes.
At the right time.

And I think the right time is just before seeding. Something has been said with regard to the condition of agriculture. I am not going back over all the figures with regard to the production of cattle, the production of hogs, the production of poultry and eggs, the production of milk and so on. But I would suggest that if one would leave out the war period in making comparisons he would probably have a much sounder basis from which to reason than if he were to continue to compare the production of some particular commodity now with its production during the- war.
For example one of the favourite criticisms which comes from the central part of the opposition is that at one time we paid the farmers to stop producing certain things. We paid them $4 an acre to take land out of wheat and put it into some other product. It is obviously unfair to compare the production of those years in livestock, which was encouraged by the payment of the $4 an acre, with production of livestock in years now, when the war is over, and we have gone back to wheat production, and when there is not that encouragement given to change over from wheat to livestock.
So I say we are on much sounder ground when we compare the results of farming in 1946 and 1947 with the results of farming in the years prior to the war, or at the latest the first two years of the war.
Does the minister not think we should diversify our agriculture in western Canada?

Yes; and if the hon. member for Melfort would make his comparison as between the present time and the time prior to the period when we were paying farmers to change over from wheat production to livestock production, he would find that the statement he made a few moments ago was quite ridiculous. I refer to his statement that the records would indicate that the government, or even the farmers themselves, have been changing over from the production of hogs to such an extent that the farmers have almost entirely gone out of hog production. That statement is not borne out by' the facts at all. Saskatchewan has not gone out of hog production. Alberta has not gone out of hog production.

Supply-Agriculture
As a matter of fact, as my hon. friend knows, during the years when we were paying western farmers to go out of grain and into livestock the provinces of western Canada produced hogs as they had never produced them before. They were producing far more hogs in the west than anyone ever expected them to produce.
Criticism has been made that we are encouraging the farmers of eastern Canada to feed western grain to hogs. Well, I am not able to follow the two criticisms as being in the interests of agriculture in this country: one to the effect that we should still be doing in western Canada what we did at the peak of the war in order to get hog production up, namely, that we should be paying to have land changed over from the production of cereals to the production of livestock, so as to have mixed farming in western Canada; and then in the next sentence, a criticism of the government for, at another period, as well as at the period in question, giving assistance to eastern farmers to encourage them to feed western grain to livestock.
My hon. friend knows as well as I do that a great many of the farmers in western Canada prefer to produce grain. Not only do they prefer to produce grain, but they think they can make more money producing grain, under ordinary circumstances. And the only one thing that took them out of grain for two or three years during the war was the fact that that grain could not be sold. We were not able to sell wheat in 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944 except to Great Britain. And we were growing much more wheat than Great Britain could eat. For that reason, and because the farmers had to have money, and because they could not get that money with their grain lying in their own bins or in elevators, we paid them to take their land out of wheat and to put it into feed grain for the purpose of feeding livestock. We told them that they should sell livestock; that they could sell it every day of the week, and get cash for it. So they did that.	.
Surely no one is suggesting that government should be carried on on a basis of that kind during a period of peace, during a period when the whole world requires and wants cereals even to the exclusion of meat in many parts of the world. They prefer to have cereals. And when we have cereals to sell, and have farmers who are producing cereals, and doing it very well, they themselves prefer to sell that grain to farmers in other parts of Canada who are going to feed it to livestock. Anyone who has lived among the farmers of western Canada knows that to be the case.
I remember the leader of the official opposition appearing in Montreal-I believe it was 5849-210
in 1938-and making a speech which appeared in the headlines across Canada, in which he stated words to the effect that this country ought to be, or was actually, divided into two areas, one west of the lakes and one east of the lakes; and that in the best interests of agriculture in this country the western farmers ought to be encouraged to produce more and more grain, while the eastern farmers ought to be encouraged to produce more and more livestock.
There is an element of truth in that. The argument was well received by farmers in both ends of Canada. We on this side of the house have sometimes said similar things; but we have never suggested that we ought to give all the assistance to people at one end of Canada, whether it was the east or the west. We have always argued that we should divide up the assistance. And if at certain times we have given assistance to western farmers to do certain things, at other times it might be in the interest of Canadian farmers that we give assistance in order to direct production into some other line.
But the most important fact in connection with anything done with regard to agriculture is the return the farmer gets. We hear a great deal about the position of agriculture, and how poorly off the farmers are. But I just wish to say that, while the farmers are not in the position, financially, in which I should like to see them right across Canada, nevertheless they will acknowledge that in all parts of Canada they are, on an average, in just a little better position at the present time than they have been at any other time in their history. I am not saying that is as good a position as they ought to be in-I repeat that statement-but they are in a little better .position at present, financially, than they have been at any other time in their history. The figures indicate that.
I am not going to go back many years. In 1941 we had about as high a return from agriculture production, on a cash basis, as we ever had in Canada up to that time. The return in that year was $967,600,000. The highest year we had ever had before that was 1928, with $1,063,000,000. Just in the second year of the war we had almost reached the highest figure we had ever had in Canada in returns from agricultural production. Then the next year we passed that highest figure. In 1942 the amount was $1,155,900,000, and the next year we went up to $1,441,000,000.

Again I repeat that I agree with members who say we ought to do all we can to see that they do better still, but I do not think it is helpful either to agriculture or to Canada to be continually saying agriculture is going down and down rather than going up and up and up, because the facts are the very opposite to those pictured by the members of the C.C.F. when they speak on this question.
I was reading the other day-and on another occasion I shall bring this to the attention of the house if the discussion follows the line which it has up to the moment-a comparison of the figures per farm in the different provinces of Canada which was put out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics only last week, from which it will be found that some statements which were made with regard to 1941 do not, as hon. members over in the Conservative section of the house were pointing out, apply to 1948. The situation in the different provinces has improved all across Canada, and I should like to say that the statistics indicate that the farmers have made more improvement in the areas which have stayed with livestock. Because of that fact, I agree with the hon. member for Melfort that we should encourage in western Canada, as far as we possibly can, the production of more and more livestock products. I agree with him that we as farmers would make more money in western Canada if we fed all our grain to livestock, but I am not so sure that we would enjoy life any better than we do farming as we are at the present time.
We have a great many farmers, just as we have a great many other people, who are not spending all their time trying to make money, and I cannot understand my hon. friends of the C.C.F., who are against anybody making profits, talking the way they do. They are not supposed to be in favour of people making profits. They speak rather in terms of people enjoying life, having an opportunity of living a fuller and a better life. I am sure there are many of us who belong to other parties who, whether we preach that doctrine or not, act that way in our living. We are not so anxious to make money as to be talking all the time of the fellow who spends all his days and nights thinking of ways of making more money. I do not agree with my hon. friends of the C.C.F. that the profiteers are living the best life in the world. I think some of us who are not spending so much time thinking about making money are getting

Do you not think we would get more out of life if we had them?

Sometimes, yes. When I go out to my farm in the summertime and find the waterworks out of condition, I have to become the chap who works down underground, but when I am in the city I do not do that. The same is true more or less about electricity on the farms. It is the simplest thing in the world to have electricity on a farm in western Canada, and I can never understand why more farmers do not have it? It does not cost half as much to have electricity on the farm in Saskatchewan as it does to own and operate a car; I do not think it costs 25 per cent as much. All you have to do in the part of western Canada in which I live is to pay $150 for a windmill-
You have the wind.

We have the wind, yes. Pay $150 for the windmill; put a generator on top of it; put a set of batteries in your basement, and you can have just as good lights as you have in this chamber. Not only that, but you can have a pressure tank to pump your water up to the top story, and not only that, you can have lights in all your buildings as well as in your home. But I think some people prefer to drive cars and do some other things rather than have what some of my hon. friends of the C.C.F. think they ought to have. My experience with farmers has been that if you give them an opportunity to do things they will do the things which they themselves think benefit them most.
I have found, during the time I have been administering a department either here or in the west, that a great many people do not take kindly to being told what they ought to do. There are things they can do, and I like to tell them some of the things that can be done, but I do not like to go so far as to say that they ought to give up some one thing on which they are spending their own money in order to invest it in something else. Oh, oh.
I have better equipment without it, and at half the cost.
Oh, no.
You had better come around and visit me some day and I shall show you.

Having said these things, I wish to complete my remarks by repeating that I do not think, in discussing these estimates, we are going to help the farmer by trying to make out that our farmers are not better off in Canada today that they were in previous times. I have a few remarks to make on various items of the agricultural estimates, but on this item I briefly wish to draw to the attention of the minister and the committee one matter that is of serious concern to the fruit industry of British Columbia, and particularly certain fruit growers in my constituency. I refer to the loss of the British preference on apples. Over a period of forty years we have been developing a fruit industry in the district which I have the honour to represent. We happen to have a particularly fine climate that produces a high quality of people and first-class fruit. For thirty years the officials of both the dominion and the provincial departments of agriculture have advised
our people, particularly those in the Kootenays, to plant certain varieties because it was proved that we could grow those possibly to better advantage than anywhere else in Canada. I refer to Cox's Orange Pippin and the Jonathan. The British people have a great liking for the Cox's Orange Pippin, while the poorer districts are fond of the Jonathan because of its medium size, high colour and solid flesh and particular flavour.
A considerable number of orchards were developed on the basis of the recommendations made by the officials of the dominion and provincial departments of agriculture. Unfortunately it is not easy to change one's horticultural habits. Over a matter of years these growers have developed orchards which produce from 1,000 to 10,000 boxes a year of these varieties. This product went largely to the British market under the benefit of the preference. The Canadian people have not to date taken to the Cox's Orange Pippin or to a great extent to the Jonathan. I mention this because it is a serious thing to the fruit industry in British Columbia and particularly to the growers of certain varieties in my district. I should like to quote from a press release on the multilateral trade agreement among seventeen countries which was issued on November 17, 1947. Dealing with the loss of this preference, it states:
Apples. One of Canada's most important contributions to the general agreement on tariffs and trade which has for its purpose the reduction of tariffs, the elimination of tariff preferences and other -trade restrictions is the relinquishing of the apple preference in the United Kingdom. Canadian apples have always enjoyed free entry into the United Kingdom market. Through the Ottawa agreement in 1932 ,a duty of 4s. fid. per hundredweight was imposed on non-empire apples. In -the 1938 trade agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom this duty was reduced to 3s. per hundredweight for the period August 16 to April 1-5. At Geneva, Canada agreed to the elimination of the apple preference during the northern hemisphere marketing season so that now apples from all sources enter the United Kingdom market free of duty from August 16 to April 15 inclusive. During the balance of the year the duty continues at 4s. 6d. per 112 pounds.
Compensation for the apple concession is obtained mainly from the United States but it cannot be matched with any single item among the United States concessions. It is a part of a mutually advantageous agreement between Canada and its neighbour and other contracting parties.
It seems to us that sufficient consideration has not been given to the position in which a considerable number of fruit growers have been placed. It would seem as though their interests had been sacrificed to some other economic interests in this country and the

United States. On January 20, 21 and 22 of this year the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association held a convention. This convention was addressed by Mr. A. K. Lloyd, chairman of Tree Fruits Limited, which is our central marketing organization. He had this to say about the imperial preference:
Under the empire trade agreement effected in 1932, we enjoyed a preference of 39 cents per box in relation to non-empire countries. In January, 1939, this was reduced to 26 cents per box.
These preferences benefited the Canadian apple industry in at least two important ways:
1.	It insured an outlet for all of the apples Canada wished to export.
2.	It obtained for Canada a higher price than was being quoted by competing countries, and while not increasing our price to the full extent of the preference, it conservatively produced from 15 cents to 20 cents per box more than would have otherwise been secured.
This empire preference, and the increased prices derived therefrom, can largely be credited with keeping the .apple industry in Canada alive during the thirties.
Under the agreement just concluded at Geneva, these preferential rates have been completely abolished, 60 that if and when there is re-entry in to the United Kingdom, Canada will be in open competition with world apple producers.
The tree fruit growers of British Columbia feel that they have not been properly considered in this matter. As I pointed out before, when a man has spent a lifetime growing certain varieties on the recommendation of dominion and provincial officials, when he has a large investment of labour and capital expended in the growing of certain varieties and then suddenly finds himself practically cut off from a market through the loss of this preference, it seems to me that he has a right to complain about not receiving sufficient consideration.
I should like the minister to explain if [DOT]\e can why our officials agreed to the loss of this preference, because apparently it was done with the consent of the Canadian officials at Geneva without any reference to the tree fruit industry of British Columbia.
