I have only a few remarks to make, which arise mainly out of the speech made by the minister. I think the minister came pretty close tonight to telling western Canada farmers that he wanted them to stay in the hog business. I think that will be surprising news to many of the farmers in the locality from which I come.
The minister also made some play, and perhaps effectively, upon the fact that hon. members to our left picture the farmers as

being in a state of semi-poverty, or words to that effect. The minister has been guilty, during the last two sessions at least, in overplaying the prosperity of the farmer. I do not .think anyone will deny that in western Canada-and perhaps this is true of all Canada-the farmers are in better shape than they have been for a long time, if not at any time in history. I think in fairness it must be admitted that the farmers had their innings coming to them after what they had gone through in the years preceding the war.
Most of the farmers' prosperity resulted from the war, but by reason of certain policies of the government, which the official opposition have criticized to a great extent they are not nearly as well off as they otherwise would have been. I think it is true to say that the farmers of western Canada have not had an opportunity to build up reserves for the years to come.
Because of a shortage of materials during the war, they were not able to obtain the mechanized equipment or to erect the buildings that they needed. If the farmers had been able to build up the reserves they needed they would have been in a position now to obtain this equipment and erect these buildings. Those reserves would have been possible if they had been allowed to secure the prices they should have got.
I do not agree with the minister when he says that hydro is not a valuable thing for the farmer.
I did not say that.
No, you did not say that.
I said it was not as valuable on my farm as what I have.

Yes. The minister preferred the windmill. But I suggest that the farmers of Manitoba, at least, would not. And so far as their judgment on that score is concerned, I am afraid, if I had to choose between the minister and the farmers of Portage plains, I would have to take the judgment of the farmers of Portage plains. They are almost fighting to get the hydro into their farms. As the hon. member for Souris reminds me, I think that is true in other parts of the country than Manitoba. I think they are entitled to the hydro, and the sooner they get it, the better off they will be. Their work will be easier and so on.
The minister has said that the farmers have had a greater gross income, and also a greater net income in the last few years than ever before in their history. I am inclined to think he is perhaps right in that, because I am sure the figures he quoted would be official figures

of some sort. I am also prepared to admit that probably he can produce figures to show that individual farmers are better off. But what is the reason for that? It is that the west, or at least in parts of it, we have had about seven exceptionally good crops which have been raised under pressure during wartime, and there has been the means of disposing of and turning those crops into cash which has boosted the returns beyond what they normally would have been. But even at that, the results are good.
But what other business similarly has not had good results? If the return is compared with that in other businesses, I do not think it will be found that the farmers have shown as great a percentage of gain as have other businesses in western Canada or in other parts of Canada. But even if they have, and even if I am entirely wrong in that argument, let us say this. The farmer today in my part of the country has the greatest capitalization he has ever had in the history of farming. He has invested more money in expensive machinery which he uses only for a short time in a year, which eliminates a good deal of expense for hired help and so on. With a combine and the field tillers and so on he can do more work with less help. His expenses have become less as a result of that. It is therefore only natural to suppose that his net will be much greater than it was ordinarily.
I think it is an important point to consider that, in order to earn the increased net about which the minister has boasted, and quite properly, the farmer's capitalization is today perhaps many times more than it was ten or fifteen years ago. Any business that increases its capitalization would be a poor one indeed if it could not increase its net, particularly when that increased capitalization has the effect of cutting down out-of-pocket expenses such as wages and so on.
I wish the minister would clarify or perhaps even retract the suggestion he makes that western Canadian farmers want to make their money the easy way; because I do not believe that in any shape or form the farmers of western Canada have ever looked for that or ever expected to make money in the easiest possible way. That old saying which perhaps prevails even yet in some parts of of the east, to the effect that the western Canadian farmers grow a big crop of wheat in a few months and then go off to California or Florida, is pretty much a shibboleth. That is a story I have heard ever since I was a boy, but I have not seen many farmers who were able, more than once in their lifetime at least, to go to California and to spend
the winter there. I do not think they would go to Florida when they could go to California if they wanted to. But I do not think that is the situation in the west. There is a certain amount of profit in it.
I am talking about western Canada.
I have not yet seen in my life a western farmer in this house who was satisfied.

That is true. Perhaps the hon. member is right. But there will come a day, if enough of us in parliament continue to stick with the western Canadian farmers, when they will get their rights and when they will be satisfied.

A suggestion has been made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie to the effect that I may have pictured the position of the farmer as being somewhat better than it is. That in itself is an indication that I do not think that nearly as large a percentage of farmers are in the income tax brackets as ought to be able to get into them. In other words, the farmers are not doing as well as some of us would like to see them do. Still the statement I made is true, that at present they are doing better than at any other time. I am not taking credit for that to the government, except to the extent that we have attempted to guide the farming community in what they are doing, in order to get returns from those who require the products we are suggesting they should produce.
That brings me to the first point raised by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, who suggested that from what I said he would take

it that I should like to see the farmers of western Canada producing more hogs at the present time. Well, that is true in a sense, but still I do not feel that at this time I should urge the farmers of western Canada to produce more hogs. The situation in the world is such that at the moment it is easier to market cereals than to market hogs. Someone may think, when I say this, that I am advising the farmers not to produce hogs, but I do not know where you can draw the line as between the two statements. The farmers will have to do that themselves.
I would say the farmer who is properly equipped to produce hogs would be very foolish to get out of that production. The farmer who went into hog production during the war period in a temporary way, without providing himself with all the necessary equipment to carry on that production in a country as cold as ours, is perhaps wise to be out of it at the present time. But I think those of us who have farmed over a period of years have generally found that it is good to take up one line of farming which is suited to the community in which we live and go ahead and produce on that basis through good times and bad. In the long run such a farmer will be better off. So I have not thought it advisable for the department or myself as minister to start advising farmers in different parts of Canada as to what they should do.
What I had in mind in suggesting that the farmer of western Canada prefers to produce grain was just that and no more. I did not intend to say anything beyond that. He does prefer it, and I do not think anyone who lives in the west would question that. He prefers to produce grain; and I quite agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie that people who go around talking about western farmers going to California do not know anything about western Canada. Only a very small percentage of the farmers of the west are able even to come and see Ottawa occasionally, let alone go to California; and some of those who are elected to the house do not always tell the correct story with respect to conditions back home.
The farming community out west is much like the farming community anywhere else. I do not think I would be fair to this house or to anyone else if I did not say that farmers, as human beings, are much like any other group of human beings; and I venture to say the majority of the farmers in this house like to make their living in the easiest way possible. When I say that I am not suggesting that the farmers are trying to avoid work, because any farmer who tries to avoid work

Supply-Agriculture
does not remain on the farm very long in this country. Work is the main thing that keeps him there.
Having said this in order to clear up any ideas that may be in the minds of those who heard the hon. member for Portage la Prairie give his impression of what I said earlier, I hope it will not be necessary later on for me to say that I have not been attempting to suggest that the farmer is making great wealth, nor have I tried to suggest that he is not as well off as people in most agricultural areas are at the present time.

I believe two or three other things should be said, and I should like to refer to the Economic Annalist, put out by the department under the minister, in relation to farmers' costs. We agree that the gross product, the physical volume, has gone up tremendously, because of rainfall and perhaps because of the Minister of Agriculture. It is pointed out here that a tremendous program was carried on by educational campaigns, plus price increases and subsidy payments, all directed at production; and the sum total of all those efforts was a tremendous increase in the physical volume of goods. Rainfall, price subsidies, the necessity of feeding the world-all these things were factors. But the farmers' costs have gone up tremendously, too. It we take the period 1935 to 1939 as the base, and the index as 100, in February, 19-18. farmers' costs stood at 170-7; so that while he has more money his real income has been reduced to that extent.
Then the farmer still needs many things. According to this report, his buildings need painting; he needs more machinery; his farm home lacks many facilities essential to the well-being of the modern farm family. I agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie; I think the minister is placing a wrong interpretation upon what the farmers like. To a farmer a car is not a luxury but part of his working equipment. He depends upon it to get his repairs; he must have it in order to run his business, and it cannot be looked upon in the same way that a car is looked upon in the life of an urban dweller. In the same way a telephone is not a luxury to a farmer; a tractor is not a luxury. The farmer has been forced to put money into these things as part of his equipment. His home also is part of his equipment, but he is not given any exemption in his income tax return on account of it. He can get an allowance with respect to a henhouse or a pigpen, but not with respect to the family home, which is just as much a part of his equipment as anything else he uses in order to remain there and produce.
I doubt whether the program for next year will show the same results as the past year or two, if the minister's own report is correct, because it points out that the size of the net income determines whether or not a farmer remains solvent. The net income in the years between 1941 and 1946 increased from 8250,000,000 to 8625,000,000; but in analysing these figures the report goes on to say that the increase was due in part to price control and subsidy programs. These price control and subsidy programs have been removed as incentives, and it is doubtful whether agriculture will be able or will want to keep up the effort to produce this volume of goods to maintain this level of income.
I do not think it should go out across Canada that the western farmer is crude or callous or does not appreciate the better things of life. As against that we have the fact that the farmer goes tb so much trouble to do the things the minister is suggesting; the fact that he will put a thousand dollars into the erection of a wind charger, and the tremendous difficulty there is in doing that sort of installation yourself. It has been particularly difficult in the last few years. If a contractor is building a block of houses in town he can get twenty bathtubs; he can get all his shingles and nails, because he is in that business; but when a farmer looks for those things he has to pay a great deal more. There is no wholesale price for him; he gets no priority. No one comes along and digs his ditches for him with a ditching machine. He digs them with a pick and shovel. He can do these things, though, if his farm income remains at a sufficiently high and stable level so that it will pay him; and incidentally they increase his production.
When the minister said a few minutes ago -the farmer did not get as much as some people think he gets, he should have said the farmer does not get as much as some people. The farmer is the man who does the hard, physical work to feed the world; and we should not forget that food is the one thing you cannot do without. You can do without a lot of people and a lot of other things, but if you run short of food you begin to die and eventually starvation gets the better of you.
I think we should demand for farmers some sort of civilization which would be complete with educational and health facilities, things that make life comfortable, things which farm families certainly earn and deserve. But we should never apologize for the farmers, and certainly we should never accept less than other people get.
Supply-Agriculture

The discussion thus far on this item has been pretty well an effort to estimate what the farmer has been receiving, or what he should receive in terms of national income. I should like to spend a few moments tonight to set out, perhaps in a somewhat broader form, what I believe we should have for ourselves, as a nation, by way of agriculture.
I believe we should first of all, set out those objectives upon which we can agree, namely the purpose for which agriculture exists. They could be classified under three headings: first, to provide food for the optimum nutrition for all our people, and to produce all possible raw materials for industry; second, to establish for all workers in agriculture, including farm operators and farm labour, a standard of living comparable with that provided in better organized urban industries, especially in relation to housing, educational opportunity and facilities, health and general culture and, third, to produce over and above our maximum needs the maximum amount of agricultural commodities for export.
If we set out those as objectives, to begin with, I think we might even surprise ourselves as to how many other things we could agree on in the House of Commons. I do not know that it does us very much good to thresh over what the farmer received back in 1940 or 1920 or 1947, if we do not make any concrete or comprehensive plan as to what the farmer may be able to receive in 1949 or 1960. I believe that is far more important.
Another factor which seems to come out of this discussion is the interdependence of agriculture generally across this country. It is so easy, as was exhibited here tonight, to get into an east versus west argument about agriculture. I cannot think of anything more futile. East or west in this country, the man who tills the soil and who produces food is attempting to make a living for himself and his family and is contributing to the wealth of the nation. It does not matter very much what type of produce he produces, or what province he happens to live in.
The fact that he is in that industry, and the further fact that that industry is the backbone of the economy of the country should be sufficient for us to treat it as a national industry, for the good of the whole nation.
As an example, in the house on many occasions we have heard about various forms of assistance for agriculture. At one time we talk about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and at another time about the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, each of which has to do chiefly with western Canada. At times

members from other parts of Canada get a little tired of providing that sort of assistance, and wonder why it is not given in other parts of Canada.

I do not know that we are tired of giving assistance, but we have to sit here so long and hear so much about it that we get pretty tired of hearing it repeated so often. We are more tired of that than of giving the actual assistance.
Do something about it, then.

I hope the hon. member will not blame those who are talking about it if there is some measure of repetition. After all, those of us on this side of the house particularly, can only suggest to the government what it should do. The government has to cany it out; and so long as the things we are suggesting have not yet been carried out, to that extent we shall have to keep on urging that it be done.
I just wished to point out that we were not-
You have been talking about tariffs for a hundred and fifty years.
I will do my own talking; you do not need to put words into my mouth.

I wish to asssure hon. members that, regardless of where they come from, I am not approaching this matter in a partisan spirit; as a matter of fact, I am trying to do the very opposite. I understand what my hon. friend means when he says that sometimes he becomes annoyed at or tired of listening to the long discussions on a subject about which he may not be particularly interested at the moment. But of course that works out both ways. And so long as we are members of the House of Commons, that is one of the penalties we have to pay for being public representatives.
An example of the interdependence of agriculture, both east and west, is the fact that while we in the west do ask taxpayers right across Canada, whether they are farmers or not, to contribute through their taxes to help us in connection with prairie farm assistance, and so on, on the other hand we are quite as cheerfully contributing to our taxes to help pay, for example, for the freight charges on feed grains going into eastern Canada. That is costing the western farmer in his tax bill a certain amount of money. Not only that, but it adds to the annoyance when he sees the feed which he himself has produced going somewhere else to feed somebody else's hogs, when he, the farmer who produced it, has to pay the freight to take it there.

Business of the House
We can understand those small sources of friction or annoyance. But I do not think they are enough to make us talk of an east-west attitude in the house.
There are many other ways in which we are interdependent. The nature of production in different parts of Canada makes us so. There are some things which can be produced on the prairies far more economically and far more conveniently than they can be produced, for example, in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick. On the other hand, potatoes can be produced in those provinces to better advantage than they can in western Canada.
What is required is not so much a piecemeal argument as to how much the farmer should get for this or that at any given time, as it is a comprehensive program designed to increase over-all production in agriculture throughout this country, through a fiscal policy which will provide an incentive to farmers to produce the goods required, and at the same time give them a certain amount of protection and stability in their prices so that they will know that they will not produce themselves right out of their own market.
We know that not long ago an international wheat agreement was agreed upon, and that it is to be ratified at a future date.
It appears, Mr. Chairman, that I shall not be able to complete my remarks this evening.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
